title: Module 1: One Health Framework
text:
WASH + One Health Integration
Water, Sanitation, Hygiene under One Health
Why WASH is Central to One Health:
WASH interventions prevent disease transmission across the human-animal-environment interface:

Safe Water: Prevents waterborne zoonoses (leptospirosis, cryptosporidiosis)
Sanitation: Breaks fecal-oral transmission of pathogens from humans and animals
Hygiene: Reduces direct contact with animal reservoirs and contaminated surfaces

One Health WASH Framework:

Integrated Water Quality Monitoring: Test for human AND animal pathogens
Livestock Waste Management: Prevent contamination of water sources
Community Hygiene: Educate on zoonotic disease prevention
Environmental Sanitation: Protect ecosystems supporting disease vectors

Source: PLOS Water Journal, “Towards a One Health approach to WASH”, 2024

Traditional WASH programs focus on human health. One Health WASH expands this to include animal health (veterinary WASH) and environmental health (ecosystem protection), recognizing that 80% of rural households in India live with livestock.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
section: Water Quality Surveillance: A One Health Application
text:
Water Quality Surveillance: A One Health Application
Integrated Monitoring Systems
Conventional Approach: - Monitor water for human pathogens only (E. coli, coliforms) - Reactive response after disease outbreaks
One Health Approach: - Monitor for human, animal, and environmental health indicators - Proactive surveillance for early warning
Example: Wastewater-Based Epidemiology (WBE)
# One Health Surveillance Data Integration
surveillance_data <- data.frame(
  Indicator = c("E. coli", "Leptospira", "Antibiotic Residues", 
                "Cryptosporidium", "Nitrate Levels"),
  Human_Health = c("High", "Medium", "High", "High", "High"),
  Animal_Health = c("Medium", "High", "High", "High", "Medium"),
  Env_Health = c("Medium", "Medium", "High", "Low", "High")
)
Application: COVID-19 wastewater surveillance detected viral RNA before clinical cases emerged, demonstrating the power of environmental monitoring for human disease.

Wastewater surveillance is a quintessential One Health tool. It monitors human pathogens (COVID, polio), animal pathogens (avian influenza), and environmental contaminants (AMR genes, heavy metals) simultaneously, providing early warning for public health interventions.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
section: Case Study: Cholera Outbreaks and One Health
text:
Case Study: Cholera Outbreaks and One Health
The Human-Animal-Environment Nexus
Background: Cholera (Vibrio cholerae) outbreaks in India often correlate with monsoon flooding and contaminated water sources.
One Health Analysis:







Component
Contributing Factors




Human
Poor sanitation, open defecation, crowded slums


Animal
Aquatic reservoirs (fish, shellfish), livestock near water sources


Environment
Flooding, water stagnation, temperature rise, algal blooms



One Health Interventions:

Human: Oral rehydration therapy, vaccination campaigns, hygiene education
Animal: Monitor aquatic animal health, regulate fish farming practices
Environment: Improve drainage, protect water sources, climate adaptation

Outcome: Integrated approach reduces cholera incidence by 60-70% compared to single-sector interventions.

The 2010 Haiti cholera outbreak demonstrated the consequences of ignoring the environment pillar. Contaminated river water (environmental failure) mixed with poor sanitation (human failure) caused a massive epidemic. One Health demands simultaneous action across all three sectors.

title: Module 1: One Health Framework
section: One Health in Climate Change Context
text:
One Health in Climate Change Context
Emerging Challenges
Climate-Water-Health Linkages:

Extreme Weather: Floods contaminate water sources, droughts concentrate pathogens
Temperature Rise: Expands vector habitats (mosquitoes, snails) in water bodies
Altered Rainfall: Disrupts seasonal water availability, increases contamination
Ecosystem Disruption: Changes animal migration patterns, spreads diseases

One Health Climate Adaptation:
# Climate-sensitive disease forecasting model
climate_factors = {
    'temperature': 'increases vector breeding',
    'rainfall': 'floods lead to waterborne disease outbreaks',
    'humidity': 'affects pathogen survival in water',
    'extreme_events': 'infrastructure damage → sanitation failure'
}
India-Specific Impacts: - Increased dengue/malaria in previously non-endemic areas - More frequent waterborne disease outbreaks post-floods - Climate refugees migrating to areas with poor WASH infrastructure

Climate change is a threat multiplier for One Health. India experienced record floods in 2023-2024, leading to major waterborne disease outbreaks. One Health preparedness requires climate-resilient WASH infrastructure and early warning systems linking meteorological and epidemiological data.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
section: WHO Guidelines for Drinking Water Quality
text:
WHO Guidelines for Drinking Water Quality
Overview and Evolution
Purpose:
Define standards for countries to develop national regulations ensuring safe drinking water supplies.
Publication History:

1984: First edition published
1993: Vol. 1 of 2nd edition
1996: Vol. 2 of 2nd edition
2011: Vol. 1 & II of 3rd edition ⭐ (current standard)
2017: Updated addendum

Key Principle:
Standards must consider local environmental, social, economic, and cultural contexts—not one-size-fits-all.
Four Aspects of Water Quality:

Acceptability aspects (Physical + Inorganic)
Microbiological aspects
Chemical aspects (Inorganic + Organic + Pesticides)
Radiological aspects


The WHO guidelines are recommendations, not mandatory regulations. Each country adapts them based on local conditions, resources, and priorities. India’s standards (IS 10500) largely align with WHO but have some variations based on endemic conditions (e.g., fluoride).

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
I. Acceptability Aspects
A. Physical Parameters
Definition: Characteristics affecting water’s aesthetic quality and acceptability to consumers.
Key Parameters:








Parameter
Acceptable Limit
Health/Aesthetic Impact




Turbidity
<5 NTU (Nephelometric Turbidity Units)
>5 NTU visible cloudiness, shields pathogens from disinfection


Colour
<15 TCU (True Colour Units)
Indicates organic matter, iron, or manganese contamination


Taste and Odour
No objectionable taste/odour
May indicate organic decay, hydrogen sulfide, or chlorination by-products


Temperature
<25°C
High temp reduces dissolved oxygen, increases microbial growth



Significance:
Even if microbiologically safe, water with poor acceptability aspects may cause consumers to seek unsafe alternative sources.

Turbidity is critical—particles shield bacteria from chlorine disinfection. Studies show that reducing turbidity from 5 NTU to 1 NTU can increase disinfection efficacy by 90%. Consumers often prefer clear water even if unsafe, rejecting turbid water even if treated.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
II. Microbiological Aspects
Bacteriological Indicators
Why Indicators?
Testing for all pathogens is impractical. Indicators signal fecal contamination and potential presence of pathogens.
Primary Indicator: Coliform Organisms

Total Coliforms: Gram-negative, lactose-fermenting bacteria (includes E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter)
Fecal Coliforms (Thermotolerant): Ferment lactose at 44°C; E. coli is the primary member
Escherichia coli: Definitive indicator of recent fecal contamination

Guideline: - Drinking water: 0 E. coli or fecal coliforms per 100 mL - Treated water entering distribution: 0 coliforms per 100 mL - Treated water in distribution: <3 coliforms per 100 mL (if chlorine residual present)
Other Indicators:

Faecal Streptococci (Enterococcus): More persistent than coliforms, indicates older contamination
Clostridium perfringens: Spore-forming; indicates remote or intermittent contamination


E. coli is the gold standard fecal indicator because: (1) exclusively of fecal origin, (2) doesn’t multiply in water, (3) easy to detect, (4) outnumbers pathogens 1000:1. However, it doesn’t indicate protozoa or viruses, which are more chlorine-resistant.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Polynuclear Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs)
Coal-Tar Contamination and Cancer Risk
What are PAHs?
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons formed during incomplete combustion of organic materials: - Coal, oil, wood, garbage burning - Vehicle exhaust - Industrial processes - Cigarette smoke
Major PAHs in Water:

Benzo[a]pyrene (BaP): Most potent carcinogen, guideline = 0.7 µg/L
Benzo[b]fluoranthene, Benzo[k]fluoranthene
Indeno[1,2,3-cd]pyrene
Dibenz[a,h]anthracene

WHO Recommendations for PAH Control:

Turbidity Reduction: PAHs adsorb to suspended particles. Reducing turbidity removes PAHs.
Ban Coal-Tar Materials: Discontinue use of coal-tar-based materials for pipe lining and storage tank coatings—major contamination source.
Source Identification: When PAH contamination detected, identify specific compounds and sources, as carcinogenic potential varies.


The 1970s-80s saw widespread PAH contamination from coal-tar pipe linings in U.S. and Europe. Decades later, elevated cancer rates appeared. WHO recommends removing old coal-tar pipes. In India, some old municipal systems still have coal-tar linings, requiring monitoring.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Health-Risk Assessment Framework
Understanding TDI, ADI, NOAEL, LOAEL
Why Risk Assessment?
Cannot test every chemical on humans ethically. Must extrapolate from animal studies to establish safe limits.
Key Concepts:
1. Tolerable Daily Intake (TDI)

Maximum amount of a substance a person can consume daily over a lifetime without appreciable health risk
Expressed as mg/kg body weight/day

2. Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI)

Similar to TDI but used for food additives and pesticides (intentional additions)
TDI used for contaminants (unintentional)

3. No-Observed-Adverse-Effect Level (NOAEL)

Highest dose in animal studies where NO adverse effects detected
Basis for deriving TDI

4. Lowest-Observed-Adverse-Effect Level (LOAEL)

Lowest dose in animal studies where adverse effects ARE detected
Used when NOAEL data unavailable (with additional uncertainty factor)


Example: Arsenic NOAEL study on rats might find 0.3 mg/kg bw/day causes no tumors. But humans may be more sensitive, so we apply uncertainty factors (typically 100-1000) to derive a safe TDI. This conservative approach protects public health given scientific uncertainties.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Uncertainty Factors (UF)
Accounting for Variability and Unknowns
Purpose:
Account for uncertainties when extrapolating from animal studies to human populations.
Four Sources of Uncertainty:








Source
Uncertainty Factor Range
Rationale




Interspecies variation
1 - 10
Animals may respond differently than humans


Intraspecies variation
1 - 10
Humans vary (children, elderly, sick more sensitive)


Adequacy of studies
1 - 10
Short-term study → lifetime exposure extrapolation


Nature/severity of effect
1 - 10
Severe effects (cancer) require more caution



Total UF Calculation:
UF (total) = UF₁ × UF₂ × UF₃ × UF₄
Typical Values:

100: Standard for well-studied chemicals (10 × 10: interspecies × intraspecies)
1000: Additional factor when using LOAEL instead of NOAEL
10,000: Maximum; higher values make TDI too imprecise (guideline becomes “provisional”)


Example: Arsenic uses UF=100 (10 interspecies × 10 intraspecies) because we have good human epidemiological data. Lead uses higher UF because children are especially vulnerable (neurodevelopment). The WHO expert panel determines UF by consensus, reviewing all available evidence.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Deriving Guideline Values Using TDI
Step-by-Step Calculation
Formula 1: Calculate TDI
TDI (mg/kg bw/day) = NOAEL (or LOAEL) / UF
Formula 2: Calculate Guideline Value (GV)
GV (mg/L) = (TDI × bw × P) / C
Where:

bw = Body weight (60 kg adult, 10 kg child, 5 kg infant)
P = Fraction of TDI allocated to drinking water (typically 0.1 or 10%)
C = Daily drinking water consumption (2 L adult, 1 L child, 0.75 L infant)

Why P = 0.1?
Most chemicals come from multiple sources (food, air, soil). Water typically contributes 10-20% of total exposure. For chemicals exclusively in water (e.g., disinfection by-products), P may be higher (0.8).

The allocation factor P is critical. For lead, P=0.5 (50%) because drinking water is a major source for infants. For pesticides, P=0.1 (10%) because food is the primary source. When deriving guideline values, we must consider all exposure routes, not just water.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Worked Example: Arsenic Guideline Value
Applying the TDI Approach
Given Data:

NOAEL (from animal studies) = 0.3 mg/kg bw/day
Uncertainty Factor (UF) = 100 (10 interspecies × 10 intraspecies)
Allocation to water (P) = 0.1 (10%)
Body weight (bw) = 60 kg (adult)
Water consumption (C) = 2 L/day

Step 1: Calculate TDI
TDI <- NOAEL / UF
TDI <- 0.3 / 100
TDI <- 0.003 mg/kg bw/day
Step 2: Calculate Guideline Value
GV <- (TDI * bw * P) / C
GV <- (0.003 * 60 * 0.1) / 2
GV <- 0.018 / 2
GV <- 0.009 mg/L = 9 µg/L
WHO Guideline: 0.01 mg/L (10 µg/L) — rounded for practical monitoring

WHO’s arsenic guideline (10 µg/L) is based on epidemiological studies in Bangladesh, Taiwan, and Chile showing skin lesions and cancers. The calculation here is simplified; actual derivation considered multiple studies, exposure routes, and cancer risk models. Some countries (Bangladesh) use 50 µg/L as an interim target due to widespread natural contamination.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
IV. Radiological Aspects
Radioactivity in Drinking Water
What is Radioactivity?
Nuclear disintegration of unstable isotopes, releasing ionizing radiation (alpha, beta, gamma particles).
Unit of Activity:

Becquerel (Bq): 1 disintegration per second (modern unit)
Curie (Ci): 3.7 × 10¹⁰ disintegrations per second (old unit)
1 Ci = 37 GBq

WHO Guideline Values:








Indicator
Guideline Value
Rationale




Gross Alpha Activity
0.5 Bq/L
Screening for α-emitters (radon, radium, uranium)


Gross Beta Activity
1.0 Bq/L
Screening for β-emitters (cesium-137, strontium-90, tritium)



If screening levels exceeded: Identify specific radionuclides and assess individual dose contribution.

Radiological contamination comes from natural (uranium, radium in rocks) or anthropogenic (nuclear facilities, medical waste) sources. Alpha emitters are more biologically damaging than beta/gamma due to high energy in short range. Radon (gas) from uranium decay in groundwater is a common concern in granite regions.

title: Module 3: Water Quality Standards & Criteria
text:
Radiological Health Effects
Somatic vs. Hereditary, Stochastic vs. Non-Stochastic
Types of Effects:
1. Somatic Effects (manifest in exposed individual) - Acute: Radiation sickness, burns (high dose, short time) - Delayed: Cancer, cataracts, cardiovascular disease
2. Hereditary Effects (affect descendants) - Genetic mutations passed to offspring - Risk increases with gonadal dose
Dose-Response Relationships:
Stochastic Effects: - Probability increases with dose (no threshold) - Severity constant - Example: Cancer risk (0.05% per mSv for solid cancers)
Non-Stochastic (Deterministic) Effects: - Severity increases with dose (threshold exists) - Example: Cataracts (threshold ~2 Gy), skin burns
Radiation Protection Principle:
Keep exposures As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA), even below guideline limits.

There’s no “safe” dose for stochastic effects (cancer)—risk exists at any exposure. Guideline values represent acceptable risk (typically <10⁻⁴ additional lifetime cancer risk). Non-stochastic effects have thresholds; below threshold, no effect occurs. Water guidelines aim to prevent deterministic effects and minimize stochastic risk.

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
SSF: The Schmutzdecke Layer
Biological Magic
What is Schmutzdecke? - Biologically active layer at sand surface - Forms naturally within 2-3 weeks - Contains: - Algae (photosynthetic) - Protozoa (predatory) - Bacteria (beneficial)
How it Works: 1. Mechanical straining - Removes large particles 2. Adsorption - Traps fine particles & some chemicals 3. Biochemical degradation - Microbes break down organics 4. Predation - Protozoa consume bacteria & viruses
Result: Enhanced pathogen removal compared to sand alone

Disinfection Method 1: Boiling
Heat-Based Inactivation
Process: - Rolling boil for 10-20 minutes - All pathogens killed at 100°C - Exception: Clostridium (sporulating organisms) may survive
Advantages: - ✓ Simple, no equipment needed - ✓ Effective against all microorganisms - ✓ No residual chemicals - ✓ Affordable (fuel-dependent) - ✓ Universal acceptance
Disadvantages: - ✗ Energy intensive - ✗ No residual protection (water recontaminates) - ✗ Taste becomes bland - ✗ Not practical for large volumes
Best Use: Individual household, emergencies, bottled water

text:
Disinfection Method 2: Chlorination
Chemical Disinfection - Most Widely Used
Forms of Chlorine: - Bleaching powder - Chlorine tablets/solution - Sodium hypochlorite - High test hypochlorite (HTH)
Typical Dosage: - Residual chlorine: 0.3-0.5 mg/L - Contact time: 30 minutes minimum - Adjusted based on water quality
Advantages: - ✓ Most widely used globally - ✓ Cost-effective - ✓ Provides residual protection - ✓ Effective against bacteria & viruses - ✓ Scalable (household to municipality)
Limitations: - ✗ Does NOT affect: HIV, Polio, Shigella, Salmonella, Cryptosporidium at normal doses - ✗ Forms disinfection by-products (DBPs) - ✗ Taste & odor (chlorine smell) - ✗ Requires careful dosing

title: Water Treatment Purification
text:
Disinfection Method 3: UV Radiation
Light-Based Inactivation
Mechanism: - UV-A/UV-C radiation damages DNA/RNA - Microorganisms cannot reproduce - Kills bacteria & viruses effectively
Advantages: - ✓ No chemicals used - ✓ No harmful by-products - ✓ Effective against most pathogens - ✓ No taste/odor changes - ✓ Rapid disinfection
Disadvantages: - ✗ No residual protection (water recontaminates during distribution) - ✗ Requires electricity - ✗ Ineffective if water turbid (particles block UV) - ✗ Higher initial cost - ✗ Lamp maintenance needed
Best Use: Small communities, household systems with post-treatment storage protection

Advanced Oxidation
Mechanism: - Ozone (O₃) oxidizes organic & microbial cell membranes - Very powerful disinfectant - Converts back to O₂ (no residue)
Effectiveness: - More effective than chlorination - Works against resistant pathogens - Removes some chemicals/odors
Advantages: - ✓ Powerful disinfection - ✓ No residual toxic by-products - ✓ Improves taste & odor
Disadvantages: - ✗ Expensive technology - ✗ No residual protection - ✗ Ozone is toxic (requires containment) - ✗ Requires skilled operators - ✗ Not suitable for small communities
Best Use: Large urban systems with other technologies

Requirements: - Clear PET plastic bottles - Sunlight exposure - Minimum 30 minutes (longer on cloudy days)

Comprehensive Oversight Activities

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 1: Source Approval
Evaluating New Water Sources
Assessment Criteria:
Quantity Assessment: - Safe yield adequate for 95% of year - Account for: Peak demand, seasonal variation, population growth - Design period: 10-50 years future projection
Quality Assessment: - Chemical analysis (heavy metals, salts) - Microbiological testing (coliforms, pathogens) - Physical parameters (turbidity, color) - Comparison with WHO standards
Feasibility Evaluation: - Available at reasonable cost - Treatability: Can be rendered safe economically - Accessibility: Proximity to population served - Sustainability: Long-term viability
Approval Decision: - Only sources meeting ALL criteria approved - Private wells require inspection & approval - Regular re-evaluation for continued suitability

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 2: Watershed Protection
Protecting Source Water Quality
Catchment Area Management: - Area draining into reservoir/water body - Primary protection zone around intake - Prevent human/animal intrusion - Restrict agricultural runoff
Prohibited Activities: - Livestock grazing near source - Human habitation upstream - Waste disposal in catchment - Industrial effluent discharge - Deforestation (increases turbidity)
Implementation Measures: - Boundary marking & fencing - Regular monitoring patrols - Community education - Legal enforcement - Vegetation maintenance
Example: Protected springs require structures preventing direct contamination

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 3: Water Works Procedures
Infrastructure Standards
Disinfection Protocols: - Plant disinfection after construction - Distribution system flushing - Regular chlorination cycles - Documentation of procedures
Routine Maintenance: - Pipe cleaning schedules - Valve inspection & repair - Reservoir cleaning (annually) - Equipment servicing
Emergency Procedures: - Pipeline break response - Contamination incident protocols - Public notification procedures - Alternative supply arrangements - Boil water advisories (when needed)
Documentation: - Maintenance logs - Test results records - Incident reports - Operator certifications

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 4: Sanitary Surveys
Field Inspection Assessment
Structural Inspection: - Source protection adequacy - Pipe integrity (no breaks, leaks) - Storage tank condition (cracks, contamination) - Treatment plant operation efficiency - Distribution network assessment
Risk Identification: - Contamination risks (sewage proximity) - Maintenance deficiencies - Operator competence issues - Treatment gaps - Cross-connection hazards
Rating System: - High risk: Immediate intervention needed - Medium risk: Corrective action plan - Low risk: Routine monitoring - No risk: Maintain standards
Follow-up: - Recommendations documented - Timeline for corrections - Re-inspection after fixes - Training for operators if needed
Frequency: - High-risk systems: Quarterly - Medium-risk: Semi-annual - Low-risk: Annual - Emergency situations: Unscheduled

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring

Surveillance Activity 5: Monitoring Programmes
Regular Water Quality Testing
Central Laboratory Services: - Analyze water samples - Equipment maintenance & calibration - Quality assurance protocols - Data management & reporting
Regional Laboratory Network: - Distributed sampling sites - Local analytical capacity - Faster turnaround time - Community access
Sampling Protocol: - Representative sampling (multiple points) - Standardized containers (sterile) - Preservation methods (chilled, chemicals added) - Chain of custody documentation - Aseptic technique (prevents contamination)
Testing Frequency: - High-risk sources: Daily or continuous - Municipal supplies: Weekly - Community systems: Monthly - Small piped systems: Quarterly - Seasonal adjustment for pollution risk

Surveillance Activity 6: Operator Certification
Personnel Competence Assurance
Training Requirements: - Basic water treatment principles - Equipment operation & maintenance - Quality testing procedures - Safety protocols - Record keeping - Emergency response
Certification Levels: - Level 1: Small piped/point systems - Level 2: Large community systems - Level 3: Municipal treatment plants - Level 4: Advanced systems with specialized technology
Educational Pathway: - Classroom theory (fundamentals) - Practical training (hands-on) - On-the-job apprenticeship - Examination & certification - Continuing education (annual/biennial)
Monitoring Operators: - Assessment visits - Performance evaluation - Troubleshooting assistance - Refresher training as needed

Surveillance Activity 7: Chemical Regulation
Treatment Chemical Management
Substances Used: - Coagulants: Alum, ferric sulfate - Disinfectants: Chlorine, ozone - pH adjustment: Lime, soda ash - Corrosion control: Phosphates, pH buffering - Sequestrants: For hardness control
Quality Standards: - Purity specifications for chemicals - Impurity limits (heavy metals, arsenicals) - Certificate of analysis required - Regular supplier audit
Dosing & Monitoring: - Calibrated equipment mandatory - Regular testing of residuals - Documentation of chemical use - Operator training on safe handling
Safety Requirements: - Proper storage facilities - Personal protective equipment - Emergency response procedures - Waste disposal protocols - Staff training

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 8: Cross-Connection Control
Preventing Backflow Contamination
What is a Cross-Connection? - Unprotected link between potable & non-potable systems - Allows contaminated water to enter drinking supply - Examples: Toilet fill pipes, fire sprinklers, industrial water
Hazards Posed: - Sewage backflow into water supply - Industrial chemicals mixing - Gray water contamination - Pathogenic microorganism introduction
Prevention Measures: - System inspection & mapping - Physical separation (best method) - Air gaps on fixtures - Check valves (one-way only) - Vacuum breakers on hose connections - Backflow prevention assemblies
Regulatory Approach: - Plumbing code requirements - Permits for new connections - Regular audits of high-risk areas - Public education - Penalties for violations

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 9: Leak Detection
Distribution System Integrity
Why Leaks Matter: - Water loss (volume, cost) - Pressure drop (invites contamination) - Ingress of pathogens into pipes - Distribution system vulnerability
Types of Leaks: - Major leaks: Visible (street flooding, puddles) - Minor leaks: Hidden (slight pressure loss) - Service line leaks: Private property - Main line breaks: System-wide impact
Detection Methods: - Acoustic listening devices - Sound of water escaping - Pressure monitoring - Drop indicates break - Flow monitoring - Night-flow analysis (demand low) - Dye tracing - Follows water path - Thermal imaging - Temperature anomalies - Ground-penetrating radar - Subsurface detection
Repair Protocol: - Isolate affected section - Excavate & repair/replace pipe - Pressure testing before reopening - Chlorine flushing post-repair - Microbiological testing - Documentation & record

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 10: Well Construction Standards
Codes of Practice for Groundwater
Site Selection: - At least 15 meters from contamination sources - Higher elevation than potential sources - Accessible for maintenance - Community consultation
Sanitary Well Construction: - Proper lining (brick, cement) to ≥6 meters depth - Parapet wall ≥70-75 cm above ground - Cement concrete platform ≥1 meter radius - Drainage slope outward - Covered top (critical for safety) - Hand pump installation with proper foundation
Deep Well Requirements: - Below first impervious layer - Professional drilling required - Strainer properly installed - Water-tight casing - Maintenance schedule
Abandonment Protocol: - Seal derelict wells to prevent contamination - Prevent standing water (mosquito breeding) - Ground-level capping minimum - Proper decommissioning documentation

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Activity 11: Plumbing Standards
Household Connection Quality
Building Connection Requirements: - Non-corrosive materials (no lead pipes) - Minimum pipe diameter maintained - Proper slope (prevents stagnation) - Isolation valves (for maintenance) - Backflow prevention at connection
In-Home Plumbing: - Separation of drinking water from sewage - No cross-connections to toilets/baths - Proper venting (prevents air locks) - Temperature control (cold water separate) - Regular inspection requirement
Storage Tank Quality: - Sanitary design (sealed, accessible) - Regular cleaning (annually minimum) - Overflow prevention - First-flush exclusion (prevents contamination) - Screening against insects
Inspection & Certification: - Plumbing permits required - Code compliance verification - Pressure testing mandatory - Chlorine flushing post-installation - Microbiological sampling

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Sampling Protocols
Aseptic Collection Techniques
Sample Container Requirements: - Sterile containers (critical for microbiology) - Glass or polycarbonate (not metal) - Sealed caps (tamper-proof) - Labeled with date, time, location - Proper volume (100-250 mL typical)
Collection Procedure: 1. Identify location - Fixed monitoring point 2. Flush line - 30 seconds (removes standing water) 3. Flame tap - Optional (kills surface bacteria) 4. Collect aseptically - Avoid touching inside container 5. Seal immediately - Prevent evaporation 6. Record metadata - Time, temperature, observer 7. Preserve sample - Chilled (4°C) or chemical additive
Transport & Storage: - Deliver within 24 hours - Keep chilled during transport - Avoid exposure to light - Document chain of custody - Note any delays or anomalies
What NOT to Do: - ✗ Do NOT rinse container (removes preservative) - ✗ Do NOT collect from just-cleaned taps - ✗ Do NOT collect in dirty containers - ✗ Do NOT leave sample at room temperature - ✗ Do NOT forget labels/documentation

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Bacteriological Surveillance
Detecting Microbial Contamination
Presumptive Coliform Test (Traditional): - Multiple tube method with lactose broth media - Gas production in tubes = presumptive positive - Confirms presence of coliforms - Limitation: Not specific to fecal origin
Confirmatory Tests: - EMB Agar: Differentiates E. coli (typical appearance) - Gram Staining: Confirms gram-negative rods - Biochemical Tests: Lactose fermentation, indole production - Culture Isolation: Identifies specific species
Membrane Filtration Technique (Modern): - Water filtered through 0.45 μm membrane - Membrane placed on selective media (mFC, mTEC) - Incubated 24 hours at specific temperature - Colonies counted directly - Advantage: Quantitative, faster, economical
Enzyme Substrate Testing (Advanced): - Presence of enzyme-substrate interaction indicates organism - Rapid results (2-4 hours) - Specific for E. coli - Used in developed countries

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Fecal Indicator Organisms
Understanding Test Interpretation
E. coli (Fecal Coliform): - Most specific fecal indicator - Human & animal intestines - Indicates recent/direct contamination - Drinking water standard: Absent (0 CFU/100mL) - If present: System failure, immediate action needed
Fecal Streptococci: - Human & animal origins (distinguishable by species) - More resistant than E. coli - Indicates: Fecal contamination (less recent) - Helps assess contamination age/source - Ratio E. coli:Strep helps determine source
Total Coliforms: - Environmental organisms (some non-fecal) - Include: E. coli + other coliforms - Indicates: Potential for contamination - Drinking water standard: Absent or <5% samples - Less specific than E. coli alone
Clostridium perfringens: - Spore-forming anaerobe - Indicates: Remote/past contamination - More resistant to treatment & disinfection - Used: To assess treatment adequacy - Especially useful for RO/UV system verification

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Colony Count Procedures
Heterotrophic Plate Count (HPC)
Purpose: - General indicator of bacterial load - Non-specific (measures total viable bacteria) - Indicates water quality broadly - Early warning system
Procedure: - Dilute water samples (10⁻¹, 10⁻², etc.) - Plate on nutrient agar media - Incubate 48 hours at 35-37°C - Count colonies (30-300 range optimal) - Calculate CFU/mL
Interpretation: - <1000 CFU/mL: Good water quality - 1000-10,000: Acceptable (investigate source) - >10,000: Indicates problem (contamination or stagnation) - Sudden increase: Potential breach in system
Limitations: - Does not identify organisms - Does not distinguish pathogenic from non-pathogenic - Temperature-dependent growth - Some organisms won’t grow on standard media

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Chemical Surveillance Testing
Monitoring Contaminant Levels
Physical Parameters: - Turbidity: Nephelometer (NTU) - Color: Spectrophotometer (TCU) - Conductivity: Electrical conductance (μS/cm) - Temperature: Thermometer (°C) - pH: pH meter (0-14 scale)
Inorganic Chemicals: - Heavy metals: Atomic absorption spectrophotometry (AAS) - Ions (chloride, fluoride, nitrate): Ion chromatography - Hardness: EDTA titration - Iron/manganese: Colorimetric methods
Disinfection Residuals: - Chlorine (free & total): DPD method (diethyl-p-phenylenediamine) - Ozone: Specific analyzer - UV dosage: Radiometer measurement
Organic Compounds: - Pesticides: Gas chromatography (GC) - PAH: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) - Volatile organics: GC-mass spectrometry

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Quality Testing Standards
Drinking Water Compliance
WHO Drinking Water Quality Guidelines:
Physical Standards: - Turbidity: <1 NTU (or <5 for systems without continuous monitoring) - Color: <5 TCU - Taste/Odor: Absent
Microbiological Standards: - E. coli: Absent (0/100 mL) - Enterococci: Absent (0/100 mL) - Enterovirus: Absent (0/100 L)
Chemical Standards: - Arsenic: 0.01 mg/L (10 μg/L) - Lead: 0.01 mg/L (10 μg/L) - Fluoride: 1.5 mg/L (upper limit) - Nitrate: 50 mg/L - (See Module 6 for complete chemical list)
Monitoring Frequency: - Microbiological: Minimum weekly (high-risk weekly, small systems monthly) - Chemical: Annual (or more if risk identified) - Physical: Daily visual, periodic testing

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Testing Methodology Gaps
Common Challenges
Infrastructure Gaps: - Limited laboratory capacity in remote areas - Expensive equipment maintenance - Shortage of trained technicians - Lack of quality control reagents
Technical Challenges: - Complex matrices interfere with testing - Environmental samples harder than pure cultures - Method validation for local conditions - Equipment calibration drift
Capacity Building Needs: - Training programs inadequate - Continuing education limited - Standardization across regions - Quality assurance protocols weak
Solutions: - Mobile laboratories - Simple field test kits (rapid testing) - Regional central labs (reference standards) - Capacity building partnerships - Digital reporting systems

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Rapid Testing Methods
Field-Level Assessment
Advantages of Rapid Tests: - Results within hours (not days) - Lower cost than laboratory testing - Portable (field deployment) - Minimal training needed - Good for screening purposes
Available Rapid Tests: - Colilert system: Most probable number (MPN) in 18-24 hours - Chromogenic substrates: Color change indicates E. coli - ATP bioluminescence: Organic matter indicator - Conductivity probes: Salinity/TDS quick assessment - Turbidity meters: Handheld devices
Limitations: - Less specific than laboratory methods - Cannot identify organisms definitively - Confirmation testing still needed for positives - Variability in technique
Best Practice: - Use rapid tests for screening - Confirm positive results in laboratory - Regular comparison with reference methods

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring

Data Management & Reporting
Surveillance Information System
Data Recording: - Date, time, location of sample - Source identification - Test results with units - Analyst name & signature - Quality assurance notes - Corrective actions taken
Database System: - Digital recording (prevent errors) - Backup systems (prevent loss) - Secure access (confidentiality) - Trend analysis capability - Report generation automated
Reporting Structure: - To water authority (daily for major issues) - To public health department (monthly) - To consumers (transparency) - To government (compliance verification) - International reporting (WHO, SDG tracking)
Public Communication: - Water quality report cards (annual) - Boil water notices (when needed) - Violation reports (transparent) - Community meetings - Website/app access to data

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Surveillance Response Protocol
When Contamination is Detected
Immediate Actions (Within Hours): 1. Verify result: Retest to confirm contamination 2. Identify source: Pinpoint location/cause 3. Assess risk: Determine population affected 4. Notify public: Issue boil water notice if needed 5. Alert authorities: Health department, water authority 6. Begin investigation: Trace contamination source
Short-term Response (24-72 hours): - Increase testing frequency - Check nearby samples (pattern analysis) - Inspect infrastructure (pipes, tanks) - Review treatment plant operation - Interview affected persons (symptom surveillance)
Corrective Actions (Days-Weeks): - Repair identified defects - Optimize treatment - Flushing/disinfection of system - Resampling to confirm resolution - Root cause analysis - Prevention measures
Communication: - Initial notice (contamination detected) - Updates on progress - All-clear notice (contamination resolved) - Post-incident review - Lessons learned documentation

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring

Advanced Surveillance Technologies
Continuous Monitoring: - On-line turbidity sensors - Chlorine residual monitors - pH continuous recording - Flow rate measurement - Unusual pattern alert systems
Wastewater Epidemiology: - Sewage sampling for pathogen detection - Early indicator of community infection - COVID-19 application (wastewater PCR) - Poliovirus surveillance - Antimicrobial resistance tracking
Syndromic Surveillance: - Hospital admission monitoring (diarrhea cases) - School absenteeism tracking - Emergency department visits - Pharmacy data (antidiarrheal sales) - Pattern recognition for outbreaks
Genomic Surveillance: - DNA sequencing of isolated pathogens - Strain tracking during outbreaks - Source attribution - Resistance mutation identification - Epidemiological investigation

title: Water Surveillance & Monitoring
text:
Case Study: Outbreak Investigation
Scenario - Cholera Detection
Initial Detection: - 15 cases of acute diarrhea in one area within 48 hours - Stool samples positive for V. cholerae - Public health alert triggered
Surveillance Actions: 1. Immediate testing: Water samples from implicated zone 2. Confirmatory testing: Coliform presence (YES - breach!) 3. Source tracing: Pipeline break near sewage line identified 4. Health response: ORS distribution, IV fluids 5. Communication: Boil water notice issued 6. Community measures: Chlorination, flushing begun
Investigation Findings: - Pipeline break at 7-meter mark - Back-pressure from sewage during low-flow period - Sewage contamination entered supply - ~2000 people affected
Corrective Actions: - Pipeline repaired (24 hours) - System flushing & chlorination (48 hours) - Microbiological testing cleared (72 hours) - All-clear issued - Root cause: Maintenance backlog
Prevention: - Pipeline replacement plan initiated - Increased monitoring frequency - Maintenance schedule intensified - Operator training reinforced

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Welcome
Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All
Learning Objectives:

Define health and describe its dimensions and the health–disease spectrum
Explain the major determinants of health using an accepted health-field model
State the Alma-Ata Declaration’s definition of Primary Health Care and its goal
Trace the evolution of medicine from curative to community medicine
Describe the Bhore Committee’s role in shaping India’s health system
Locate “Health for All” within the later MDG → SDG trajectory

How to read this deck: each slide is tagged and color-coded — 🟢 MUST KNOW (core, exam-critical), 🟡 SHOULD KNOW (important context), 🟣 MAY KNOW (enrichment), and 🧡 QUESTION (self-check).

This chapter opens the Foundations section. It sets up vocabulary and frameworks — the definition of health, its determinants, and Primary Health Care — that every later chapter in this series assumes.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
What Is Health?
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO Constitution (1948):

“Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.”

This definition has never been formally amended. Two things make it radical for its time:

It rejects the purely biomedical view (health = absence of disease)
It names three dimensions at once — physical, mental, social — as jointly necessary


Drafted at the International Health Conference, New York, 1946; the WHO Constitution entered into force on 7 April 1948 (now marked annually as World Health Day).
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Dimensions of Health
🟢 MUST KNOW


Commonly taught dimensions:

Physical — normal structure and function of the body
Mental — a state of balance with oneself and one’s environment
Social — harmony with the social fabric: family, community, work
Spiritual — a sense of purpose, values, or belief
Emotional — the ability to recognize and appropriately express feelings


Why this matters:
A person can be free of diagnosable disease and still not be “healthy” by this definition — e.g. someone who is physically fit but socially isolated or under chronic mental distress.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
The Health–Disease Spectrum
🟢 MUST KNOW
Health is not a fixed state but a continuum, moving in both directions:
Death → Chronic illness → Disability → Mild sickness → No obvious illness → Positive health

Positive health is more than “not sick” — it implies resilience and a reserve capacity to cope with physical, biological, and social stress
Any individual can move along this spectrum over time; public health aims to shift populations toward the positive-health end, not just treat people once they’ve crossed into illness
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Determinants of Health
🟢 MUST KNOW
A widely used health-field model groups the determinants of health into four domains:







Domain
Examples




Environment
safe water, sanitation, housing, air quality, occupational hazards


Heredity / Biology
genetic makeup, age, sex, inherited susceptibility to disease


Lifestyle / Behaviour
diet, physical activity, tobacco/alcohol use, personal hygiene


Health services
access, affordability, and quality of preventive and curative care



Key implication: health care services are only one of four determinants — and historically not the largest one. Improving population health depends at least as much on environment, behaviour, and social conditions as on hospitals and doctors.

This is the Blum / Lalonde-style “health field concept,” standard across Indian community-medicine teaching. Different sources add socio-economic and political factors as a fifth domain — mention this as a natural extension in discussion, not a contradiction.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Primary Health Care: Alma-Ata, 1978
🟢 MUST KNOW
At Alma-Ata (in present-day Kazakhstan), 134 WHO member states and 67 organisations adopted a declaration defining Primary Health Care (PHC):

“Essential health care based on practical, scientifically sound and socially acceptable methods and technology, made universally accessible to individuals and families… through their full participation and at a cost the community and country can afford… the first level of contact of individuals, the family and community with the national health system.”

The goal it set: “Health for All by the year 2000” — a level of health that would let all people lead a socially and economically productive life, with PHC declared the key strategy to reach it.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Principles of Primary Health Care
🟢 MUST KNOW

Equitable distribution — care reaches rural and underserved populations, not just cities
Community participation — individuals and communities help plan and run their own care, not just receive it
Intersectoral coordination — health links to agriculture, education, housing, water supply, and rural development
Appropriate technology — methods that are scientifically valid, affordable, and acceptable to the community, not merely the most advanced available
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
Evolution of Medicine
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Medicine’s scope has widened in stages:

Curative medicine — treating disease in the individual patient
Preventive medicine — stopping disease before it starts (e.g. immunization, screening)
Social medicine — recognizing that disease has social causes and consequences, not only biological ones
Community medicine / Public health — shifting the unit of concern from the individual patient to the community as a whole

Each stage didn’t replace the one before it — modern health systems practice all four simultaneously, for different needs.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
The Bhore Committee (1946)
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The Health Survey and Development Committee, chaired by Sir Joseph Bhore, was appointed by the colonial government in 1943 and reported in 1946. It remains the foundational blueprint for independent India’s health system.
Key recommendations:

Integrate preventive and curative services at every administrative level, instead of running them separately
Establish Primary Health Centres — short-term target of one PHC per 40,000 population
Strengthen maternal and child health services
Reorient medical education toward training “social physicians” — doctors trained in preventive and social medicine, not curative care alone
Raise health spending to at least 15% of government expenditure

Many of these ideas — the PHC network, integration of services — are still the structural basis of India’s public health system today.
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
section: From Health for All to the SDGs
text:
From Health for All to the SDGs
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
“Health for All by 2000” was not fully achieved by its target year, but it set a template that later global goals built on:

2000–2015: Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) — several goals (child mortality, maternal health, HIV/malaria/TB) were direct descendants of the Health for All agenda
2015–2030: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) — health consolidated under SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, with Universal Health Coverage (UHC) as an explicit target

(The MDG → SDG transition is covered in depth in Millennium Development Goals to SDGs; this slide only places it on the timeline.)
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
India’s National Health Policy Milestones
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

NHP 1983 — first National Health Policy; reaffirmed Health for All through a PHC-centred approach
NHP 2002 — revised targets in light of slower-than-planned progress; emphasized decentralization and public–private partnership
NHP 2017 — shifted emphasis toward Universal Health Coverage, preventive and promotive care, and raising public health spending as a share of GDP
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
A Longer View of Medicine
🟣 MAY KNOW

Hippocrates (Ancient Greece, c. 460–370 BCE) — separated medicine from religion and superstition; the source of the Hippocratic Oath’s ethical tradition
Sushruta (Ancient India) — author of the Sushruta Samhita, an early foundational text of surgery and Ayurvedic medicine
Public-health thinking is not a modern invention: sanitation and water-management systems appear in ancient urban civilisations (e.g. the Indus Valley), long before “public health” was named as a field
crumbs: Man and Medicine: Towards Health for All

title: Man and Medicine
text:
The Social Gradient of Health
🟣 MAY KNOW
Health outcomes follow a gradient across socioeconomic position, not just a gap between “poor” and “rich”: at every step up the social ladder, average health tends to improve. This is associated with the work of Michael Marmot and the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health.
Implication: improving population health requires acting on the “causes of the causes” — income, education, working conditions — not only on medical risk factors.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
Welcome
Concept of Health and Disease
Learning Objectives:

Define disease and distinguish it from illness and sickness
Describe the epidemiological triad of agent, host, and environment
Explain the natural history of disease and its phases
Describe the iceberg phenomenon of disease
Apply the levels of prevention — primordial, primary, secondary, tertiary
Distinguish Koch’s postulates from the Bradford Hill criteria of causation

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter builds directly on Chapter 1’s determinants-of-health framework: here we formalize how disease actually develops and how prevention maps onto that process.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
Disease, Illness, and Sickness
🟢 MUST KNOW
These three words are often used interchangeably but mean different things in community medicine:

Disease — an objective, measurable deviation from normal structure or function of the body, detectable by clinical or laboratory means
Illness — the subjective experience of feeling unwell, as perceived by the person themselves
Sickness — the social dimension: society’s recognition that a person is unwell (e.g. being excused from work)

Why the distinction matters: a person can have disease without illness (asymptomatic infection), or feel ill without demonstrable disease — both are relevant to how and when a health system responds.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
The Epidemiological Triad
🟢 MUST KNOW
Disease results from an interaction between three factors:


Agent
The factor whose presence (or excess/deficiency) is necessary for disease — biological (bacteria, virus), chemical, physical, nutritional, or mechanical

Host
The organism that harbours disease — human factors like age, sex, immunity, genetics, and behaviour affect susceptibility

Environment
External conditions that bring agent and host together — physical, biological, and socio-economic environment

Disease occurs when this triad is out of balance — a change in any one factor can tip the balance toward or away from disease.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
Natural History of Disease
🟢 MUST KNOW
The natural history of disease is how a disease would progress over time without any intervention — from first cause to final outcome. It has two broad phases:

Pre-pathogenesis phase — the disease agent exists in the environment, but has not yet entered the human host; risk factors are accumulating
Pathogenesis phase — begins once the agent enters a susceptible host: incubation → early (subclinical) pathogenesis → clinical disease → outcome (recovery, disability, or death)

Key idea: prevention is most effective the earlier it acts in this timeline — this is exactly what the levels of prevention (next slides) are built around.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
The Iceberg Phenomenon
🟢 MUST KNOW
Clinically diagnosed cases in a community are often only the visible tip of the true disease burden:
Visible: clinically diagnosed, reported cases Hidden (below the surface): sub-clinical, undiagnosed, and unreported cases — often the majority
Implication: relying only on reported/diagnosed cases underestimates the real scale of a disease in a population — this is why screening and active surveillance matter (screening is covered in a later Foundations chapter).

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
Levels of Prevention
🟢 MUST KNOW
Prevention is classified by when it intervenes in the natural history of disease:








Level
Target
Example




Primordial
Prevents risk factors from ever emerging
Anti-tobacco social norms in children who don’t smoke yet


Primary
Prevents disease onset in exposed/at-risk people
Vaccination, health education


Secondary
Detects and treats disease early, before it’s clinically obvious
Cancer screening, early diagnosis


Tertiary
Limits disability and aids rehabilitation once disease is established
Physiotherapy after stroke, disease-management programs



Exam tip: Primordial ≠ Primary. Primordial acts on risk factors before they exist; Primary acts once risk/exposure is already present but before disease develops.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
Multifactorial Causation
🟢 MUST KNOW
Most disease — especially non-communicable disease — does not have a single cause. The web of causation model shows disease arising from an interconnected network of contributing factors (biological, behavioural, environmental, social), rather than one agent producing one disease.
Contrast with infectious disease: classical infectious disease causation (one specific agent → one specific disease) is closer to a single-cause model — which is exactly what Koch’s postulates were built to test.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
Koch’s Postulates
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Robert Koch’s 19th-century criteria for proving a microorganism causes a specific disease:

The organism must be found in all cases of the disease, and absent in healthy individuals
It must be isolated from the diseased host and grown in pure culture
The cultured organism must reproduce the disease when introduced into a healthy, susceptible host
The organism must be re-isolated from that newly infected host and shown to be identical to the original

Limitation: doesn’t work for viruses, asymptomatic carriers, or diseases with multiple contributing causes — one reason Bradford Hill’s criteria were later developed for broader causal inference.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
Bradford Hill Criteria of Causation
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Sir Austin Bradford Hill (1965) proposed nine viewpoints to judge whether an association found in epidemiological studies is likely causal:

Strength of association
Consistency across studies/populations
Specificity of the effect
Temporality — cause precedes effect (the only criterion considered truly essential)
Biological gradient — dose–response relationship
Plausibility
Coherence with existing knowledge
Experiment — evidence from intervention/removal of the exposure
Analogy with similar known causal relationships

Used for: non-communicable disease and environmental exposures, where Koch’s postulates don’t apply.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
Risk Factors
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
A risk factor is any attribute, exposure, or characteristic that increases the probability of disease, without necessarily being a sufficient or direct cause.

Non-modifiable — age, sex, genetic makeup, family history
Modifiable — smoking, diet, physical inactivity, blood pressure, occupational exposure

Public health prevention strategy focuses on modifiable risk factors, since non-modifiable ones can only inform risk stratification, not intervention.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
Sufficient-Component Cause Model
🟣 MAY KNOW
Rothman’s “causal pie” model refines the web-of-causation idea: a disease occurs only when a sufficient cause — a full “pie” made of several component causes — is complete. The same disease can have multiple different sufficient causes (multiple different pies), each built from different combinations of components. Removing just one component (a “necessary cause,” if it appears in every pie) can prevent the disease even without knowing every other component.

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
From Miasma to Germ Theory
🟣 MAY KNOW

Miasma theory (dominant until the 19th century) — believed disease spread through “bad air” from decomposing matter; still drove genuinely useful sanitation reforms
Germ theory (Pasteur, Koch, late 19th century) — established that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases, replacing miasma theory and giving rise to modern microbiology and Koch’s postulates

title: Concept of Health and Disease
text:
Syndemics: A Modern Extension
🟣 MAY KNOW
A syndemic is the concept that two or more diseases (or a disease and a social condition) cluster together and interact within a population, each worsening the other — for example, the interaction between undernutrition, poor sanitation, and infectious disease in the same vulnerable communities. It extends the web-of-causation idea from a single disease to interacting epidemics.

title: Principles of Epidemiology

Welcome
Principles of Epidemiology
Learning Objectives:

State the standard definition of epidemiology and its core aims
Distinguish ratio, proportion, and rate
Define incidence and prevalence, and the relationship between them
Describe descriptive epidemiology by person, place, and time
Outline the broad types of epidemiological study
Recognize John Snow’s 1854 investigation as a founding case study

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter gives the vocabulary and basic measures that Chapter 4 (Epidemiologic Methods) will use to compare exposed and unexposed groups, and that Chapter 5 (Screening) will use to evaluate tests.

title: Principles of Epidemiology
text:
What Is Epidemiology?
🟢 MUST KNOW
John Last’s definition (1988), the standard reference definition:

“The study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to the control of health problems.”

Three ideas packed into this definition:

Distribution — who gets disease, where, and when (descriptive)
Determinants — why they get it (analytical)
Application — using that knowledge to control and prevent disease

title: Principles of Epidemiology
text:
Aims of Epidemiology
🟢 MUST KNOW

Describe the distribution and magnitude of health problems in populations
Identify the etiology (causes and risk factors) of disease
Predict trends and the future disease burden
Evaluate the effectiveness of interventions, programs, and health services
Provide the evidence base to guide health policy and planning

title: Principles of Epidemiology
text:
Ratio, Proportion, and Rate
🟢 MUST KNOW
These three terms are frequently confused but are mathematically distinct:








Term
Definition
Numerator in denominator?




Ratio
Relation of one quantity to another
No — numerator and denominator are separate groups


Proportion
A ratio where the numerator is a subset of the denominator
Yes


Rate
A proportion with a time dimension built in
Yes, plus time



Example: “3 males per 2 females” is a ratio; “60% of the class is male” is a proportion; “12 new cases per 1,000 population per year” is a rate.

title: Principles of Epidemiology
text:
Incidence
🟢 MUST KNOW
Incidence measures how many new cases of disease occur in a population over a defined period:
Incidence Rate = (Number of new cases during a period) / (Population at risk over that period)

Measures risk — the probability of developing disease
Requires following a population forward in time
Best measure for studying disease causation (etiology)

title: Principles of Epidemiology
text:
Prevalence
🟢 MUST KNOW
Prevalence measures how many existing cases (old + new) there are at a given time — it does not distinguish when each case began:
Prevalence = (Number of existing cases) / (Total population)

Point prevalence — cases at one specific point in time
Period prevalence — cases at any time during a defined interval

Relationship (steady state): Prevalence ≈ Incidence Rate × Average Duration of Disease
A disease can have high prevalence but low incidence if it lasts a long time (e.g. diabetes) — prevalence and incidence answer different questions and must not be confused.

title: Principles of Epidemiology
text:
Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place, Time
🟢 MUST KNOW
Descriptive epidemiology characterizes who, where, and when disease occurs — the first step before asking why (analytical epidemiology):

Person — age, sex, occupation, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, behaviour
Place — urban vs. rural, national/international variation, local clustering
Time — secular (long-term) trends, seasonal patterns, cyclical patterns, and point-source (epidemic) patterns

title: Principles of Epidemiology
text:
Types of Epidemiological Studies (Overview)
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Three broad categories — detailed study designs are covered in Epidemiologic Methods:

Descriptive — describes distribution (person/place/time); generates hypotheses but cannot test them
Analytical — tests hypotheses by comparing exposed vs. unexposed groups (e.g. cohort, case-control studies)
Experimental — the investigator actively assigns exposure/ intervention (e.g. randomized controlled trials)

title: Principles of Epidemiology
text:
Uses of Epidemiology
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Assessing the community’s health status and identifying its health problems
Studying the natural history and prognosis of disease
Identifying syndromes by describing clinical patterns
Completing the clinical picture of chronic diseases by finding sub-clinical and mild cases
Searching for causes of disease by comparing rates in different population subgroups
Evaluating the effectiveness and efficiency of health services and interventions

title: Principles of Epidemiology
text:
Time Patterns of Disease
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Secular trend — gradual change in disease frequency over years to decades (e.g. declining infectious disease, rising NCD burden)
Seasonal trend — regular, predictable variation tied to season (e.g. diarrheal disease peaking in summer/monsoon)
Cyclical trend — periodic variation over a few years (e.g. some vaccine-preventable diseases before mass immunization)
Point epidemic — a sharp spike from a common source over a short period (e.g. a contaminated water source)

title: Principles of Epidemiology
section: John Snow and the Broad Street Pump
text:
John Snow and the Broad Street Pump
🟣 MAY KNOW
In 1854, a severe cholera outbreak in London’s Soho district killed over 600 people in about ten days. John Snow, rejecting the then-dominant miasma (“bad air”) theory, mapped cholera deaths by address and traced them to a single water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded local authorities to remove the pump handle — after which the outbreak subsided. The contamination was later traced to a leaking sewer near the pump’s well.
Why it matters: this is widely regarded as the founding case study of modern epidemiology — using spatial/descriptive data to identify a cause and act, before germ theory or laboratory confirmation existed.

title: Principles of Epidemiology
text:
Population at Risk
🟣 MAY KNOW
The denominator used in incidence and prevalence calculations should, strictly, be the “population at risk” — people who could potentially develop the disease being studied (e.g. excluding already-immune or already-affected individuals, or using only women for cervical cancer incidence). Using the wrong denominator is a common source of error in interpreting epidemiological rates.

Learning Objectives:

Calculate attributable risk and attributable risk percent
Describe the design and purpose of a randomized controlled trial
Distinguish selection bias, information bias, and confounding

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter builds directly on Chapter 3’s incidence/prevalence and the overview of study-design categories, going into the analytical and experimental designs in depth.

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
The 2×2 Table
🟢 MUST KNOW
Every analytical epidemiological comparison starts from a 2×2 table of exposure vs. outcome:




Disease +
Disease −




Exposed
a
b


Unexposed
c
d



All of the measures on the following slides — relative risk, odds ratio, attributable risk — are calculated directly from these four cell counts (a, b, c, d).

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
Cohort Study
🟢 MUST KNOW
Design: starts with a disease-free population, divides it by exposure status, and follows both groups forward in time to compare who develops disease.

Prospective cohort — exposure and outcome measured going forward from now
Retrospective cohort — exposure already recorded in the past; outcome is determined by looking forward from that point

Direct measure obtained: incidence in both groups → Relative Risk (RR)
RR = [a / (a+b)] / [c / (c+d)]
RR > 1 suggests increased risk with exposure; RR = 1 suggests no association; RR < 1 suggests a protective effect.

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
Case-Control Study
🟢 MUST KNOW
Design: starts with people who already have the disease (cases) and people who don’t (controls), then looks backward to compare their past exposure.

Cannot calculate incidence directly (cases are already selected) — so RR cannot be measured directly
Instead calculates the Odds Ratio (OR):

OR = (a × d) / (b × c)
Rare disease assumption: when the disease is uncommon (roughly <10% in the unexposed group), OR closely approximates RR — this is why case-control studies are widely used to estimate risk for rare diseases.

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:

🟢 MUST KNOW




Cohort

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
Attributable Risk
🟢 MUST KNOW
Attributable Risk (AR) is the excess risk in the exposed group that is directly due to the exposure — the risk difference:
AR = Risk in exposed − Risk in unexposed
Attributable Risk Percent (AR%) expresses this as a proportion of the total risk in the exposed group — i.e. how much of the exposed group’s risk would be eliminated if the exposure were removed:
AR% = [(Risk exposed − Risk unexposed) / Risk exposed] × 100
Contrast with RR: RR tells you the strength of an association; AR/AR% tells you the public health impact of removing the exposure.

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT)
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Design: the investigator actively and randomly assigns participants to an intervention group or a control/comparison group, then follows both forward to compare outcomes.

Randomization balances known and unknown confounders between groups — the key strength of the RCT design
Blinding (single/double) reduces information bias from participants or assessors knowing group assignment
Considered the strongest design for establishing causation, but often impractical or unethical for harmful exposures (you cannot randomize people to smoke, for instance — hence cohort/case-control designs exist)

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
Cross-Sectional and Ecological Studies
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Cross-sectional study — measures exposure and disease simultaneously, at a single point in time, in a population; useful for estimating prevalence, but cannot establish which came first (exposure or disease) — the key limitation
Ecological study — compares exposure and disease rates across groups/populations, not individuals (e.g. comparing national smoking rates to national lung cancer rates); fast and cheap, but vulnerable to the ecological fallacy — a group-level association doesn’t guarantee the same association holds for individuals

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
Selection Bias
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Occurs when the individuals selected into a study are not representative of the population they’re meant to reflect — e.g. volunteer bias, or a hospital-based control group that differs systematically from the general population.
Must be prevented at the design stage — it generally cannot be fixed by statistical adjustment after data are collected.

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
Information Bias
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Arises from inaccurate measurement of exposure or outcome — including:

Recall bias — cases (who are searching for an explanation for their illness) may remember or report past exposures differently than controls — a particular risk in case-control studies
Observer/interviewer bias — differential data collection depending on which group a participant is in

Like selection bias, this is best prevented by design (blinding, standardized measurement) rather than fixed afterward.

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
Confounding
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
A confounder is a third factor that is associated with both the exposure and the outcome, and distorts the apparent exposure–disease association — it can exaggerate, mask, or even reverse the true direction of an effect.
Example: age can confound the association between grey hair and heart disease — older people have more grey hair and more heart disease, with no direct causal link between the two.
Unlike selection and information bias, confounding can be addressed after data collection — through stratification, matching, or statistical adjustment (e.g. multivariable regression) — as well as through randomization at the design stage.

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
Ecological Fallacy — A Closer Look
🟣 MAY KNOW
The ecological fallacy is the specific error of assuming that a correlation observed at the group/population level must also hold at the individual level. A classic teaching example: countries with higher average chocolate consumption have been shown to have more Nobel laureates per capita — an association at the national level that says nothing about whether any individual eating more chocolate is more likely to win a Nobel Prize.

title: Epidemiologic Methods
text:
Number Needed to Treat
🟣 MAY KNOW
Number Needed to Treat (NNT) is a clinically-oriented extension of attributable risk, used mainly for trial results: the number of patients who need to receive an intervention for one additional patient to benefit, calculated as the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction (NNT = 1 / AR, expressed as risk difference).

Welcome

Learning Objectives:

Define screening and distinguish it from diagnosis

Calculate and interpret sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV
Describe the main types of screening
Explain lead time bias, length time bias, and overdiagnosis

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter closes the Foundations section by applying the incidence/ prevalence and 2x2-table thinking from Chapters 3–4 to the specific problem of evaluating a screening test and a screening program.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
What Is Screening?
🟢 MUST KNOW
Screening is the presumptive identification of unrecognized disease in apparently healthy, asymptomatic individuals, using tests that can be applied rapidly and economically to a large population.
Screening is NOT diagnosis:

A screening test sorts people into “likely disease” vs. “unlikely disease” — it does not confirm disease
Everyone who screens positive must still undergo a proper diagnostic test to confirm or rule out the condition

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Wilson and Jungner Criteria (1968)
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO’s ten classic principles for deciding whether a condition is suitable for a screening program:

The condition should be an important health problem
There should be an accepted treatment for recognized disease
Facilities for diagnosis and treatment should be available
There should be a recognizable latent or early symptomatic stage
There should be a suitable test for that early stage
The test should be acceptable to the population
The natural history of the condition should be adequately understood
There should be an agreed policy on whom to treat
The cost of case-finding should be economically balanced against overall medical care spending
Case-finding should be a continuing process, not a one-time project

title: Screening for Disease
text:
The Screening 2×2 Table
🟢 MUST KNOW
Every screening test is judged against a reference/gold-standard diagnosis:




Disease +
Disease −




Test +
True Positive (TP)
False Positive (FP)


Test −
False Negative (FN)
True Negative (TN)



All four validity measures on the next slides come directly from this table.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Sensitivity and Specificity
🟢 MUST KNOW
Sensitivity — the ability to correctly identify people who have the disease:
Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN)
Specificity — the ability to correctly identify people who do not have the disease:
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)
Key property: both are properties of the test itself and do not depend on how common the disease is (prevalence) in the population tested.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Predictive Values
🟢 MUST KNOW
Positive Predictive Value (PPV) — given a positive test, the probability the person actually has disease:
PPV = TP / (TP + FP)
Negative Predictive Value (NPV) — given a negative test, the probability the person is actually disease-free:
NPV = TN / (TN + FN)
Key property: unlike sensitivity/specificity, PPV and NPV do depend on disease prevalence — the same test will have a lower PPV in a low-prevalence population, even with unchanged sensitivity/specificity.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Types of Screening
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Mass screening — offered to an entire population, regardless of individual risk (e.g. a national program)
Selective/targeted screening — offered only to a high-risk subgroup (e.g. screening smokers for lung disease)
Multiphasic screening — several screening tests applied together in one session (e.g. a health camp offering blood pressure, blood sugar, and vision checks together)
Opportunistic screening — offered to a person who is already seeking care for an unrelated reason

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Lead Time Bias
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Lead time is the interval between detection by screening and the point when the disease would normally have been diagnosed clinically (from symptoms).
Lead time bias occurs when screening appears to prolong survival — because the clock on “survival” starts earlier — even if the person dies at exactly the same actual time as they would have without screening.
Why it matters: raw survival-time comparisons between screened and unscreened groups can be misleading unless lead time is accounted for.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Length Time Bias and Overdiagnosis
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Length time bias — screening preferentially detects slow-growing, less aggressive disease, because it is present and detectable for longer; fast-growing, aggressive disease is more likely to cause symptoms and be diagnosed clinically between screening rounds. This makes screened cases look like they have better outcomes, independent of any real benefit.
Overdiagnosis — the extreme case: screening detects a genuine abnormality that would never have caused symptoms or harm in the person’s lifetime, leading to unnecessary labeling and treatment.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Sensitivity–Specificity Trade-off
🟣 MAY KNOW
For a test with a continuous or graded result (e.g. a blood level), the cutoff chosen to define “positive” trades sensitivity against specificity: lowering the cutoff to catch more true cases (higher sensitivity) also increases false positives (lower specificity), and vice versa. This trade-off is often visualized with a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, used to choose an optimal cutoff.

title: Screening for Disease
text:
Choosing Between Screening Designs
🟣 MAY KNOW
Mass screening is efficient for a common, serious, and well-understood condition (e.g. blood pressure), but wasteful and potentially harmful (overdiagnosis, false positives, anxiety) for rare conditions — reinforcing why the Wilson–Jungner criteria (importance, natural history, economic balance) matter before launching a program, not just whether a test technically exists.
