🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter applies Chapter 2’s levels of prevention and Chapter 3’s epidemiological triad specifically to infectious disease, and opens the Diseases section of the curriculum.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
The Chain of Infection
🟢 MUST KNOW
Communicable disease transmission depends on six linked elements — break any one link, and transmission stops:

Infectious agent — the causative organism
Reservoir — where the agent lives and multiplies (human, animal, or environment)
Portal of exit — how the agent leaves the reservoir (respiratory tract, gut, skin, blood)
Mode of transmission — how it travels to a new host
Portal of entry — how it enters the new host
Susceptible host — an individual capable of being infected

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Modes of Transmission
🟢 MUST KNOW


Direct transmission

Direct contact (touch, sexual contact)
Droplet spread (coughing, sneezing, over short distance)
Transplacental (mother to fetus)


Indirect transmission

Vehicle-borne — contaminated water, food, fomites
Vector-borne — via an insect/arthropod (mechanical or biological)
Airborne — droplet nuclei or dust suspended in air over distance

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Reservoirs of Infection
🟢 MUST KNOW

Human reservoir — a case (symptomatic) or a carrier (asymptomatic but infectious)
Animal reservoir — diseases transmitted from vertebrate animals to humans are called zoonoses
Environmental reservoir — soil, water (e.g. tetanus spores in soil, Legionella in water systems)

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Basic Reproduction Number (R₀)
🟢 MUST KNOW
R₀ is the average number of secondary infections produced by one infected person in a completely susceptible population.

R₀ > 1 → each case generates more than one new case → epidemic potential
R₀ < 1 → the outbreak is expected to die out
R₀ = 1 → disease remains endemic at a steady rate

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Herd Immunity
🟢 MUST KNOW
Herd immunity is indirect protection of susceptible individuals when a sufficiently high proportion of a population is immune, breaking chains of transmission even for those who aren’t immune themselves.
Herd immunity threshold (HIT):
HIT = 1 − (1 / R₀)
Example: a disease with R₀ = 3 needs roughly two-thirds (66%) of the population immune to interrupt sustained transmission.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
section: Levels of Prevention Applied to Communicable Disease
text:
Levels of Prevention Applied to Communicable Disease
🟢 MUST KNOW
Chapter 2’s levels of prevention map directly onto infectious disease control:







Level
Communicable disease example




Primordial
Improving sanitation and housing before any outbreak risk exists


Primary
Immunization, vector control, safe water


Secondary
Case detection, contact tracing, early treatment


Tertiary
Rehabilitation from disease sequelae (e.g. post-polio care)

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Isolation vs. Quarantine
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Isolation — separating a person already known to be infected (diagnosed or symptomatic) from others, until no longer contagious
Quarantine — separating a person who was exposed but is not yet known to be infected, for the duration of the incubation period, to see if disease develops

Both are control measures acting on different links of the chain of infection — isolation removes an active reservoir; quarantine interrupts transmission from a potential future case.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Secondary Attack Rate
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Secondary Attack Rate (SAR) measures how contagious a disease is within a close-contact group (e.g. a household), following exposure to a primary case:
SAR = (New cases among contacts) / (Total susceptible contacts)
Related concept — incubation period: the time between exposure to an infectious agent and the first appearance of symptoms; it determines how long quarantine should last.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Outbreak Investigation: The 10 Steps
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The standard CDC-style sequence for investigating a suspected outbreak:

Prepare for field work
Establish the existence of an outbreak
Verify the diagnosis
Define and identify cases
Describe data by time, place, and person
Develop hypotheses
Evaluate hypotheses
Refine hypotheses / conduct additional studies
Implement control and prevention measures
Communicate findings

(In practice these steps often overlap and don’t run strictly in order — control measures, for instance, are often started well before the investigation formally concludes.)

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Emerging and Re-emerging Infections
🟣 MAY KNOW

Emerging infectious diseases — newly identified, or newly significant, infections in a population (e.g. a novel pathogen)
Re-emerging infectious diseases — previously controlled diseases that increase again (e.g. due to declining vaccination coverage, antimicrobial resistance, or ecological change)

Both categories are driven by similar factors: urbanization, travel, climate change, land-use change, and breakdowns in public health infrastructure.

title: Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases
text:
Smallpox Eradication
🟣 MAY KNOW
Smallpox remains the only human disease ever declared eradicated (WHO, 1980), achieved through a global vaccination campaign combined with surveillance-containment (“ring vaccination” around each detected case) rather than mass vaccination alone. It remains the reference case study for what a successful global eradication program requires: an effective vaccine, no animal reservoir, and a recognizable, short-lived infectious stage.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Welcome
Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
Learning Objectives:

Define non-communicable disease (NCD) and name the four major NCDs
Identify the four shared modifiable behavioural risk factors
Distinguish behavioural from metabolic/intermediate risk factors
State the global NCD targets (WHO 25x25 and SDG 3.4)
Describe the WHO STEPS surveillance approach
Explain Rose’s population strategy vs. high-risk strategy

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

Chapter 6 covered communicable disease; this chapter is its structural mirror for non-communicable disease, and reuses the levels-of-prevention and causation frameworks from the Foundations section.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
What Is a Non-Communicable Disease?
🟢 MUST KNOW
An NCD is a disease that is not directly transmissible from person to person, and typically has a long duration and slow progression, resulting from a combination of genetic, physiological, environmental, and behavioural factors.
The four major NCDs (responsible for the large majority of the global NCD burden):

Cardiovascular disease (CVD)
Cancer
Chronic respiratory disease
Diabetes mellitus

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
section: The Four Shared Behavioural Risk Factors
text:
The Four Shared Behavioural Risk Factors
🟢 MUST KNOW
The same four modifiable behaviours drive all four major NCDs, which is why NCD prevention is tackled as one integrated agenda rather than disease-by-disease:

Tobacco use
Unhealthy diet
Physical inactivity
Harmful use of alcohol

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Metabolic (Intermediate) Risk Factors
🟢 MUST KNOW
Behavioural risk factors act through measurable, intermediate biological changes:

Raised blood pressure
Overweight / obesity
Hyperglycaemia (raised blood glucose)
Hyperlipidaemia (raised blood cholesterol/lipids)

These metabolic factors are themselves the direct targets of most clinical NCD screening and management.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Global NCD Targets
🟢 MUST KNOW

WHO “25×25” target — a 25% relative reduction in premature mortality (ages 30–69) from the four major NCDs by 2025, compared with 2010 levels
SDG Target 3.4 — reduce premature NCD mortality by one-third by 2030 (relative to 2015), and promote mental health and well-being

“Premature” mortality in both targets specifically means death in the 30–69 age band — deaths that public health intervention can plausibly prevent.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Non-Modifiable Risk Factors
🟢 MUST KNOW
Alongside the four modifiable behaviours, NCD risk is also shaped by factors that cannot be changed:

Age — NCD risk rises with age for most conditions
Sex — some NCDs show marked sex differences in incidence
Genetics / family history — inherited susceptibility

Public health strategy focuses on the modifiable factors, but non-modifiable factors still matter for risk stratification and targeted screening.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
WHO STEPS Surveillance
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The WHO STEPwise approach to Surveillance (STEPS) is the standard method countries use to monitor NCD risk factors, in three progressively more intensive steps:

Step 1 — Questionnaire: demographic data and behavioural risk factors (tobacco, alcohol, diet, physical activity)
Step 2 — Physical measurements: height, weight, waist circumference, blood pressure
Step 3 — Biochemical measurements: blood glucose and lipid levels

Countries can implement Step 1 alone or build up to all three, depending on resources.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Population Strategy vs. High-Risk Strategy
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Geoffrey Rose (1981) distinguished two prevention strategies:

High-risk strategy — identify and intervene on individuals at highest risk (e.g. treating severe hypertension)
Population strategy — shift the risk-factor distribution of the entire population slightly downward (e.g. a national salt-reduction policy)

Rose’s Prevention Paradox: because most cases of a common disease arise from the large number of people at moderate risk (not the small number at extreme risk), a population-wide strategy usually prevents more total disease than a high-risk strategy — even though the benefit to any one individual is small.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Double Burden of Disease
🟣 MAY KNOW
Many low- and middle-income countries, including India, now face a double burden of disease: they have not fully controlled communicable, maternal, and nutritional conditions, while NCDs are simultaneously rising — meaning health systems must manage both agendas at once, with finite resources.

title: Epidemiology of Chronic Non-Communicable Diseases
text:
Measuring NCD Burden: DALYs
🟣 MAY KNOW
The overall burden of a disease — combining both fatal and non-fatal impact — is commonly measured using Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs): years of healthy life lost to premature death plus years lived with disability. NCDs, being long-duration and disabling rather than always immediately fatal, are a major driver of global DALY burden. (Health indicators, including DALYs, are covered in more depth in the Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics chapter.)

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Welcome
Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
Learning Objectives:

Define essential medicines and state WHO’s selection criteria
Describe India’s National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
State WHO’s definition of rational use of medicines and list forms of irrational use
Distinguish substandard, falsified, and generic medicines
Explain why WHO retired the term “counterfeit medicines”

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter shifts focus from disease epidemiology to the medicines supply chain — access, rational prescribing, and quality — as a determinant of health-system performance.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
What Are Essential Medicines?
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO definition: essential medicines are those that satisfy the priority health care needs of a population.
Selection criteria:

Disease prevalence and public health relevance
Evidence of clinical efficacy and safety
Comparative cost and cost-effectiveness

The first WHO Model List of Essential Drugs was published in 1977, with 186 medicines, to help countries prioritize which medicines to stock, procure, and make affordable at every level of care.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
section: India’s National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
text:
India’s National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
🟢 MUST KNOW
India adapts the WHO model into its own National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), maintained under the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) — India’s National Regulatory Authority.

First published 2011; most recently revised as NLEM 2022 (384 medicines across 27 therapeutic categories)
Inclusion criteria: approved/licensed in India, cost-effective, and stable under Indian storage conditions
Purpose: ensure accessibility of affordable, quality medicines at every level of healthcare, and to guide public procurement and price control

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Rational Use of Medicines
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO definition (1985): rational use means patients receive medications appropriate to their clinical needs, in doses that meet their individual requirements, for an adequate period of time, and at the lowest cost to them and their community.
The core criteria:

Appropriate indication
Appropriate medicine choice
Appropriate dosage
Correctly dispensed
Patient appropriately informed
Patient adherence

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Forms of Irrational Use
🟢 MUST KNOW
Common patterns of irrational medicine use:

Polypharmacy — using too many medicines per patient
Inappropriate use of antimicrobials (wrong dose, for non-bacterial infections) — a major driver of antimicrobial resistance
Over-use of injections where oral formulations would work
Prescribing that doesn’t follow clinical guidelines
Inappropriate self-medication, often with prescription-only drugs
Non-adherence to prescribed dosing regimens

Scale of the problem: WHO estimates more than half of all medicines worldwide are prescribed, dispensed, or sold inappropriately, and half of all patients fail to take them correctly.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Substandard and Falsified Medical Products
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
In 2017, the World Health Assembly retired the term “counterfeit medicines” in favour of Substandard and Falsified (SF) medical products:

Substandard — authorized medical products that fail to meet quality standards or specifications
Falsified — products that deliberately and fraudulently misrepresent their identity, composition, or source

Why the term changed: “counterfeit” is a legal/intellectual-property concept (trademark infringement) and doesn’t necessarily indicate a health risk. The new terms reframe the issue as a public health problem, separate from patent and trademark disputes.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Generic vs. Branded Medicines
🟡 SHOULD KNOW

Branded/innovator medicine — sold under a manufacturer’s trademark, often while under patent protection
Generic medicine — a bioequivalent copy of an approved medicine, sold under its chemical/generic name (or a different brand) once patent protection expires, typically at much lower cost

Generic substitution is one of the most effective, low-cost levers for improving access to essential medicines — most NLEM medicines are available generically.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
Access to Medicines: Broader Determinants
🟣 MAY KNOW
Beyond the essential-medicines list itself, actual access depends on:

Rational selection and use (covered above)
Sustainable financing and affordable pricing
Reliable health and supply systems (procurement, storage, distribution — including cold-chain where needed)
Sound regulatory systems to keep substandard/falsified products out of the supply chain

These four pillars are the standard WHO framework for describing access to essential medicines as a health-system, not just a pharmacological, issue.

title: Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines
text:
The 2017 SSFFC-to-SF Terminology Shift
🟣 MAY KNOW
Before 2017, WHO used the unwieldy acronym SSFFC (Substandard/Spurious/Falsely-labelled/Falsified/Counterfeit) medical products. This was simplified to SF (Substandard and Falsified) at the Seventieth World Health Assembly specifically to separate the public health question (is this medicine safe and effective?) from intellectual-property law (is this a trademark violation?) — two questions that had previously been conflated under one confusing label.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Welcome
Nutrition and Health
Learning Objectives:

Distinguish undernutrition, overnutrition, and the double burden of malnutrition
Compare kwashiorkor and marasmus as forms of protein-energy malnutrition
Define stunting, wasting, and underweight using WHO Z-score criteria
Name the major micronutrient deficiency disorders
Outline India’s flagship nutrition programme structure (ICDS → POSHAN Abhiyaan → Saksham Anganwadi & Poshan 2.0)

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter connects the NCD chapter’s “double burden” language to nutrition specifically, and gives the anthropometric vocabulary (stunting/wasting/underweight) used throughout Indian public-health program monitoring.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Malnutrition: The Spectrum
🟢 MUST KNOW
Malnutrition covers deficiencies, excesses, or imbalances in a person’s intake of energy and/or nutrients — it is not only about “too little”:

Undernutrition — wasting, stunting, underweight, and micronutrient deficiencies
Overnutrition — overweight, obesity, and diet-related NCDs

Double burden of malnutrition: the coexistence of undernutrition and overnutrition — across a population, within the same household, and even within the same individual over their lifetime (e.g. a stunted child who later becomes an obese adult).

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Protein-Energy Malnutrition: Marasmus
🟢 MUST KNOW
Marasmus — PEM without edema — results from an overall calorie deficiency (inadequate intake of all nutrients, especially energy).
Clinical picture: severe muscle wasting, depletion of body fat, low weight-for-height, reduced mid-upper arm circumference, a head that looks disproportionately large, dry skin, thin hair, and irritability.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Protein-Energy Malnutrition: Kwashiorkor
🟢 MUST KNOW
Kwashiorkor — PEM with edema — results primarily from severe dietary protein deficiency, despite near-adequate energy (calorie) intake.
Clinical picture: peripheral pitting edema, “moon facies,” maintained or increased body fat, hepatomegaly, dry/peeling skin, and apathy.
A mixed form (marasmic-kwashiorkor), combining features of both, also occurs.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Anthropometric Indicators of Undernutrition
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO Child Growth Standards classify undernutrition using Z-scores (standard deviations from the median of a healthy reference population), each below −2 SD:








Indicator
Reflects
Type




Stunting (low height-for-age)
Chronic undernutrition
Long-term


Wasting (low weight-for-height)
Acute undernutrition
Short-term


Underweight (low weight-for-age)
Both chronic and acute
Composite



Exam tip: underweight is a composite measure and can result from either stunting, wasting, or both — it doesn’t tell you which.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Major Micronutrient Deficiencies
🟢 MUST KNOW

Vitamin A deficiency — the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness (xerophthalmia); also increases infection mortality
Iron deficiency anaemia — the most common micronutrient deficiency globally, particularly affecting women and children
Iodine deficiency disorders (IDD) — ranging from goitre to irreversible cognitive impairment (cretinism) if deficient during pregnancy/infancy

Each has a dedicated national control program in India (Vitamin A Prophylaxis, National Iron Plus Initiative, National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme).

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
India’s Nutrition Programme Architecture
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
India’s flagship child/maternal nutrition support has evolved through three stages:

ICDS (1975) — Integrated Child Development Services, India’s original flagship programme for children 0–6 years and pregnant/ lactating mothers, delivered through Anganwadi Centres
POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018) — India’s National Nutrition Mission; universalized and better-integrated ICDS with other nutrition schemes, aiming for measurable reductions in stunting, wasting, and anaemia
Saksham Anganwadi & Poshan 2.0 (2021–26) — the current umbrella scheme, merging ICDS, POSHAN Abhiyaan, the Scheme for Adolescent Girls, and the National Crèche Scheme into one integrated nutrition support programme

(Broader health-programme structures and financing are covered in Health Programmes in India.)

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Growth Monitoring
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Regular growth monitoring — plotting a child’s weight and height against standard growth charts over time — is a core Anganwadi/primary care activity, because:

It detects faltering growth early, before overt clinical malnutrition develops
It is a surveillance tool, not just an individual diagnostic one — aggregated data guide district- and state-level nutrition programming
It links directly to the iceberg phenomenon (Chapter 2): most undernutrition in a community is sub-clinical unless actively measured

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Undernutrition’s Long-Term Link to NCDs
🟣 MAY KNOW
WHO notes that undernutrition early in life — including in utero — may predispose a person to overweight and non-communicable diseases like diabetes and heart disease later in life (the “fetal origins” or Barker hypothesis). This is part of why the double burden of malnutrition is described as occurring across an individual’s life course, not only across a population at one point in time.

title: Nutrition and Health
text:
Body Mass Index (BMI)
🟣 MAY KNOW
For adults, nutritional status is commonly screened using Body Mass Index (BMI) = weight (kg) / height² (m²), with WHO cutoffs of underweight (<18.5), normal (18.5–24.9), overweight (25–29.9), and obese (≥30) — though these cutoffs are population-level screening tools, not a substitute for individual clinical assessment.

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter closes the Diseases section by extending Chapter 1’s dimensions-of-health framework (physical, mental, social, …) into a full treatment of mental health as a public health priority in its own right, not an afterthought to physical disease.

title: Mental Health
text:
What Is Mental Health?
🟢 MUST KNOW
WHO definition: mental health is a state of mental well-being that enables people to cope with the stresses of life, realize their abilities, learn and work well, and contribute to their community.

Mental health has both intrinsic and instrumental value, and is recognized as a basic human right
It exists on a continuum, experienced differently by each person — directly echoing Chapter 2’s health–disease spectrum concept
A combination of individual, family, community, and structural factors can either protect or undermine it at any given time

title: Mental Health
text:
The Burden of Mental Disorders
🟢 MUST KNOW
Common mental disorders — depression, anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and substance use disorders — together contribute a very large share of the global burden of disease when measured in DALYs, because they are long-duration and disabling rather than usually immediately fatal (recall Chapter 7’s point about NCDs and disability).
Key structural problem — the treatment gap: in most countries, especially low- and middle-income ones, the majority of people with a diagnosable mental disorder never receive any formal treatment.

title: Mental Health
text:
National Mental Health Programme, India (1982)
🟢 MUST KNOW
India launched its National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) in August 1982, one of the first countries to do so at national scale, with three core objectives:

Ensure availability and accessibility of minimum mental healthcare for all, especially the most vulnerable and underprivileged
Encourage application of mental health knowledge in general healthcare and social development
Promote community participation in mental health service development

title: Mental Health
text:
District Mental Health Programme (DMHP)
🟢 MUST KNOW
Piloted in Bellary district, Karnataka (1985–1990) by NIMHANS — offering outpatient services, a small inpatient facility, referral services, education/awareness, and community screening — and formally added to the NMHP in 1996.
Significance: DMHP demonstrated that basic mental healthcare could be delivered through the general primary health care system, at the district and primary-health-centre level, rather than requiring specialized psychiatric hospitals alone — a direct application of the Alma-Ata primary health care principles from Chapter 1.

title: Mental Health
text:
Mental Healthcare Act, 2017
🟢 MUST KNOW
India’s Mental Healthcare Act (2017) shifted the legal framework toward a rights-based approach, including:

The right to access mental healthcare as a legal entitlement
Advance directives — a person can specify, in advance, how they wish (or don’t wish) to be treated during a future mental health crisis
Section 115 — a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress unless proven otherwise, and shall not be tried or punished under the Indian Penal Code’s suicide-attempt provision; the state instead has a duty to provide care, treatment, and rehabilitation

Effect of Section 115: it doesn’t formally repeal the underlying IPC provision, but makes prosecution for a suicide attempt practically impossible, reframing it as a health issue rather than a crime.

title: Mental Health
section: WHO mhGAP: Closing the Treatment Gap
text:
WHO mhGAP: Closing the Treatment Gap
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
WHO’s Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP), launched in 2008, responds to the wide gap between mental health needs and available resources, especially in LMICs, through task-shifting/task-sharing:

Trains non-specialist health workers (general nurses, doctors, community health workers) to identify and manage common mental, neurological, and substance-use conditions
Uses standardized, evidence-based intervention guides so care doesn’t depend on scarce specialist psychiatrists alone

This is the mental-health-specific application of the same resource-constrained, primary-care-centred logic behind DMHP.

title: Mental Health
section: Stigma as a Public Health Barrier
text:
Stigma as a Public Health Barrier
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Stigma — negative attitudes and discriminatory behaviour toward people with mental illness — is one of the strongest barriers to seeking and receiving mental healthcare, operating at multiple levels:

Public stigma — societal prejudice and stereotyping
Self-stigma — internalized shame that discourages help-seeking
Structural stigma — discriminatory policies, laws, or institutional practices (which the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 explicitly tries to reduce)

title: Mental Health
section: Community Mental Health vs. Institutional Care
text:
Community Mental Health vs. Institutional Care
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Global mental health policy — including India’s DMHP model — has shifted away from long-term custodial care in isolated psychiatric institutions, toward community-based mental health services: outpatient clinics, primary-care integration, day-care centres, and family/community support — improving both access and the person’s ability to remain integrated in their community, consistent with the “social” dimension of health from Chapter 1.

title: Mental Health
section: Suicide as a Public Health Issue
text:
Suicide as a Public Health Issue
🟣 MAY KNOW
Suicide is treated in modern public health policy as a preventable public health outcome, not solely an individual or moral failing — reflected in the Mental Healthcare Act’s shift from criminalization to care. Prevention strategies span means restriction, crisis helplines, media reporting guidelines, and integrating suicide-risk screening into routine primary care.

section: Common Mental Disorders: A Brief Overview
text:
Common Mental Disorders: A Brief Overview
🟣 MAY KNOW

Depression — persistent low mood and loss of interest/pleasure, the single largest contributor to years lived with disability globally
Anxiety disorders — excessive fear or worry disproportionate to actual threat
Bipolar disorder — alternating episodes of depression and mania
Schizophrenia — a severe disorder involving distortions in thinking, perception, and behaviour
Substance use disorders — harmful or dependent use of alcohol or other psychoactive substances

title: Health Programmes in India
text:
Welcome
Health Programmes in India
Learning Objectives:

Describe the structure of the National Health Mission (NRHM + NUHM)
Explain Ayushman Bharat’s two-pillar design
Outline the RMNCH+A strategy and its “+A” additions
Distinguish vertical from horizontal (integrated) programme design
Recognize where nutrition- and mental-health-specific programmes fit into this wider architecture

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

Nutrition programmes (ICDS/POSHAN) and mental health programmes (NMHP/ DMHP) were already covered in the Diseases section. This chapter gives the umbrella architecture they sit inside, rather than repeating their detail.

title: Health Programmes in India
text:
National Health Mission (NHM)
🟢 MUST KNOW
NHM is India’s umbrella public health programme, envisioning universal access to equitable, affordable, and quality health care that is accountable and responsive to people’s needs. It has two sub-missions, unified under one governance structure in 2013:

National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) — launched 2005; a fully functional, community-owned, decentralized rural health delivery system, with inter-sectoral convergence on water, sanitation, education, and nutrition alongside health services
National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) — extends the same logic to urban poor and slum populations

Key NRHM strategy: deploying an ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) in every village as a community-level link to the health system.

title: Health Programmes in India
text:
Ayushman Bharat: Two Pillars
🟢 MUST KNOW
Launched 2018, Ayushman Bharat moves from a segmented approach to a continuum-of-care model, built on two pillars:

Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs) — upgrading Sub Centres and Primary Health Centres to deliver Comprehensive Primary Health Care, including maternal/child health, NCD screening, and free essential drugs and diagnostics, close to where people live
Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) — financial protection for secondary and tertiary hospitalization, covering about 40% of India’s households (the poorest and most vulnerable), for ~1,400 procedures at empanelled public and private hospitals

title: Health Programmes in India
text:
RMNCH+A Strategy
🟢 MUST KNOW
RMNCH+A (Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health) is India’s strategic framework for reducing maternal and child morbidity/mortality, launched following the 2013 “Call to Action” summit.
What the “+A” adds:

Adolescence as its own distinct life stage, not folded into “child” or “adult” care
Explicit linkage of maternal/child health to reproductive health, family planning, and adolescent-specific needs
A continuum of care — linking community-based and facility-based services with referral pathways between levels, rather than treating each life stage in isolation

title: Health Programmes in India
text:
Vertical vs. Horizontal Programme Design
🟢 MUST KNOW

Vertical programme — a disease- or condition-specific programme with its own dedicated staff, budget, and management structure (e.g. an older-style single-disease control programme)
Horizontal (integrated) programme — delivered through the general health system’s existing infrastructure and staff, serving multiple health needs together

The trend in India: NHM, Ayushman Bharat, and RMNCH+A all represent a deliberate shift toward horizontal integration — delivering multiple services (maternal care, NCD screening, nutrition, mental health) through the same primary-care platform, rather than parallel vertical programmes competing for the same frontline worker’s time.

title: Health Programmes in India
text:
Where Other Chapters’ Programmes Fit
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
This umbrella architecture is where the programme-specific chapters covered earlier connect in:

ICDS / POSHAN Abhiyaan / Saksham Anganwadi & Poshan 2.0 (Nutrition chapter) — nutrition-specific service delivery, converging with NHM’s broader RMNCH+A goals
NMHP / DMHP (Mental Health chapter) — mental health integrated into the same district/primary-care system that NRHM’s decentralization strategy was built to strengthen

Exam tip: don’t re-derive nutrition or mental-health programme detail here — this chapter is about the container, not the contents.

title: Health Programmes in India
text:
Financing and Governance Structure
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
NHM operates through a multi-level governance structure:

National level — policy direction, overall financing norms
State level — State Health Missions adapt national guidelines to local context
District and sub-district level — implementation, service delivery, and bottom-up feedback

Flexible financing (states can allocate NHM funds against locally identified priorities, within national norms) is a deliberate design choice to accommodate India’s wide state-to-state variation in health system starting points.

title: Health Programmes in India
text:
Health Committees and Community Ownership
🟣 MAY KNOW
NRHM’s design explicitly builds in community ownership mechanisms — village and facility-level health committees that give local communities a voice in planning and monitoring services, alongside frontline workers like ASHAs — reflecting the same “community participation” principle from the Alma-Ata Declaration (Chapter 1).

title: Health Programmes in India
text:
Scale of PM-JAY
🟣 MAY KNOW
PM-JAY is frequently described as one of the world’s largest government-funded health assurance schemes by number of beneficiary households targeted, illustrating the scale challenge unique to India’s health financing: designing a single scheme workable across enormous diversity in population density, disease burden, and existing health infrastructure across states.

Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
Learning Objectives:

List the 8 Millennium Development Goals and identify the three explicitly health-focused ones
State the key SDG 3 health targets
Explain why the global development agenda moved from MDGs to SDGs
Distinguish the scope and design philosophy of the two frameworks

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

Chapter 1 already placed “Health for All” on the MDG->SDG timeline, and Chapter 7 already introduced SDG 3.4 in the NCD context. This chapter gives the full picture both of those referenced without repeating either.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
The Eight Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015)
🟢 MUST KNOW

Eradicate extreme poverty and hunger
Achieve universal primary education
Promote gender equality and empower women
Reduce child mortality
Improve maternal health
Combat HIV/AIDS, malaria, and other diseases
Ensure environmental sustainability
Develop a global partnership for development

Three goals were explicitly health-focused: Goals 4, 5, and 6 — though several others (poverty/hunger, environment, global partnership) were also tracked using health-related indicators.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
Key MDG Health Targets
🟢 MUST KNOW

Goal 4 (child mortality): reduce the under-five mortality rate by two-thirds between 1990 and 2015
Goal 6 (HIV/AIDS, malaria, other diseases): halt and begin to reverse the spread of HIV/AIDS by 2015; achieve universal access to HIV treatment by 2010; halt and begin to reverse malaria and other major diseases by 2015

Result: the MDGs galvanized unprecedented global attention, funding, and accountability on this focused set of concerns, with substantial — though incomplete — progress by 2015.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
The Seventeen Sustainable Development Goals (2015–2030)
🟢 MUST KNOW
Adopted by all UN member states in September 2015, the SDGs comprise 17 goals and 169 targets, applying universally to all countries (not only low- and middle-income countries, as the MDGs largely did).
Health sits at SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being — “ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages” — with 13 targets covering a much broader spectrum than the three MDG health goals.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
Key SDG 3 Targets
🟢 MUST KNOW

Maternal mortality: reduce the global ratio to below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030
Child mortality: end preventable newborn/under-5 deaths — targets of ≤12 neonatal deaths per 1,000 and ≤25 under-5 deaths per 1,000 live births
Communicable disease: end the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and neglected tropical diseases, and combat hepatitis and water-borne disease
SDG 3.4: reduce premature NCD mortality by one-third, and promote mental health (introduced already in the NCD chapter)
Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and access to safe, effective medicines and vaccines for all
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
Why the Agenda Broadened
🟡 SHOULD KNOW









MDGs
SDGs




Scope
8 goals, narrowly focused
17 goals, 169 targets, broad


Applies to
Primarily developing countries
Universally, all countries


Process
Perceived as top-down (set by experts/UN)
Developed through inclusive, participatory consultation


Health coverage
3 goals: child, maternal, infectious disease
1 goal (SDG 3), but covering both communicable AND non-communicable disease, injuries, and UHC



The shift reflects a recognition that health outcomes depend on interlocking sectors (poverty, education, environment, inequality) — consistent with the multifactorial-causation and social-determinants ideas from earlier chapters.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
Criticism of the SDG Approach
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The SDGs’ breadth is also their most common criticism: with 17 goals and 169 targets, analysts argue the framework is less focused and harder to measure than the MDGs, risking diffused attention and resources across too many priorities at once — a direct trade-off against the MDGs’ narrower, more trackable design.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
The Paradigm-Shift Challenges
🟣 MAY KNOW
Achieving the SDG 3 health agenda has been described as requiring a genuine paradigm shift across five challenges: intersectoral leadership on the structural drivers of health, shifting focus from treatment to prevention, addressing commercial determinants of ill-health (e.g. tobacco, alcohol, ultra-processed food industries), integrating rights-based approaches, and strengthening civic engagement and accountability.
crumbs: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals

title: Millennium Development Goals to Sustainable Development Goals
text:
India’s MDG-to-SDG Transition
🟣 MAY KNOW
India, alongside other countries, undertook a formal national consultation process on transitioning its own monitoring and planning systems from MDG to SDG indicators — reflecting that the SDGs, unlike the MDGs, require every country (not only lower-income ones) to track and report progress against the same global framework.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
Welcome
Demography and Family Planning
Learning Objectives:

Describe the four stages of the demographic transition model
Define and distinguish CBR, CDR, TFR, GRR, and NRR
Explain replacement-level fertility
Trace the history of India’s family planning programme, 1952 to present
State the goal of India’s National Population Policy 2000

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter gives the demographic vocabulary that underlies population- level health planning, and traces India’s role as a pioneer in national family planning policy.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
The Demographic Transition Model
🟢 MUST KNOW
A generalized description of how birth rates, death rates, and population growth change as a society moves from pre-industrial to industrialized, in four stages:

Stage 1 — High birth rate, high death rate → slow/stable growth (pre-industrial)
Stage 2 — Death rate falls (better sanitation/medicine), birth rate stays high → rapid population growth
Stage 3 — Birth rate begins to fall (urbanization, education, contraception) → growth slows
Stage 4 — Low birth rate, low death rate → stable population

Where most transitions stall or reverse today: some countries now describe a Stage 5, where birth rate falls below death rate, causing population decline — not part of the classical four-stage model but increasingly relevant.

title: Demography and Family Planning
section: Crude Birth Rate and Crude Death Rate
text:
Crude Birth Rate and Crude Death Rate
🟢 MUST KNOW
Crude Birth Rate (CBR) — live births per 1,000 mid-year population in a given year.
Crude Death Rate (CDR) — deaths per 1,000 mid-year population in a given year.
Both are “crude” because they don’t adjust for the population’s age or sex structure — a country with an older population will show a higher CDR even with excellent health care, simply due to demographics.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
Total Fertility Rate
🟢 MUST KNOW
Total Fertility Rate (TFR) — the average number of children a woman would bear over her lifetime, if she experienced the current age-specific fertility rates throughout her childbearing years.
Replacement-level fertility — the TFR at which a population exactly replaces itself across generations (approximately 2.1 in most settings, accounting for child mortality and the sex ratio at birth). A country with TFR consistently below this level will eventually see its population decline, absent migration.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
Gross and Net Reproduction Rate
🟢 MUST KNOW

Gross Reproduction Rate (GRR) — like TFR, but counts only daughters a woman would have — a measure of generational replacement through the female line, ignoring mortality
Net Reproduction Rate (NRR) — refines GRR further by also adjusting for the probability that daughters survive to their mother’s childbearing age; NRR = 1 means the population is exactly replacing itself generation to generation

Exam tip: GRR ignores mortality; NRR accounts for it — this is the key distinguishing feature between the two.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
India’s Family Planning Programme: Origins
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
In 1952, India became the first country in the world to launch an official national family planning programme, aiming to reduce birth rates “to stabilize the population at a level consistent with the requirements of the national economy.”

1966 — a separate Department of Family Planning created within the Ministry of Health
1977 — following the coercive sterilization controversies of the Emergency period, the new government’s population policy explicitly ruled out compulsion, making the programme purely voluntary — a landmark and lasting policy shift

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
National Population Policy 2000
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
India’s National Population Policy (NPP) 2000 set its goals around:

Addressing unmet need for contraception
Providing free and compulsory school education up to age 14
Reducing infant and maternal mortality
Achieving population stabilization by 2045

NPP 2000 implementation was later integrated with the National Rural Health Mission (launched 2005) as the operational vehicle for delivering its goals, connecting demography policy directly to the health-systems architecture from Chapter 11.

title: Demography and Family Planning
section: Age Structure and the Population Pyramid
text:
Age Structure and the Population Pyramid
🟣 MAY KNOW
A population pyramid — a bar chart of population by age and sex — visually reflects a country’s demographic-transition stage: a wide base (many young people) indicates high fertility (early transition), while a more rectangular shape indicates low fertility and an ageing population (late transition). India’s own age structure varies significantly by state, reflecting different transition stages within one country.

title: Demography and Family Planning
text:
Demographic Dividend
🟣 MAY KNOW
The demographic dividend is the potential economic growth benefit that can arise when a country’s working-age population (15–64) is proportionally larger than its dependent population (children and elderly) — typically occurring during the middle stages of the demographic transition, as fertility falls but before the population ages substantially. Realizing this dividend depends on adequate education, employment, and health investment during that window.

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

crumbs: Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

title: Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics
text:
Antenatal Care: The WHO 2016 Model
🟢 MUST KNOW
In 2016, WHO increased its recommended antenatal care from 4 to a minimum of 8 contacts, scheduled at approximately 12, 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38, and 40 weeks of gestation — one contact in the first trimester, two in the second, and five in the third.
Purpose: provide respectful, individualized, person-centred care at every contact, combining effective clinical interventions with timely information and psychosocial/emotional support — not just a checklist of tests.
crumbs: Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

title: Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics
text:
High-Risk Pregnancy
🟢 MUST KNOW
A high-risk pregnancy is one with pre-existing or current conditions that raise the risk of complications for mother, fetus, or newborn. Risk factors fall into five broad categories:

Demographic — age under 18 or over 35
Adverse pregnancy history — previous miscarriage, stillbirth, or complication
Medical complications — hypertension, diabetes, kidney/autoimmune/ thyroid disease
Pregnancy-related conditions — arising during the current pregnancy
Environmental/social determinants — poverty, poor nutrition, low education, unstable housing

Early identification — ideally at the first antenatal contact — allows special monitoring and referral before complications become severe.
crumbs: Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

title: Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics
text:
The Under-Five Clinic
🟢 MUST KNOW
The Under-Five Clinic (adapted from the Western “well-baby clinic” concept) is a single access point delivering preventive, promotive, curative, referral, and educational services together for children under five.
The symbolic triangle used to teach this concept:

Apex — care during illness (curative)
Left side — adequate nutrition
Right side — immunization
Central inner triangle — family planning
Border line — health education for the mother

The WHO Decade of Healthy Ageing (2021–2030)
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Proclaimed by the UN in December 2020, following WHO endorsement, with the vision that all people live longer, healthier lives. Its four action areas:

Changing how we think, feel, and act toward age and ageing
Developing communities that foster older people’s abilities
Delivering person-centred, integrated care and primary health services responsive to older people
Providing access to long-term care when needed

Explicitly aligned with the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda’s principle of “leaving no one behind” (Chapter 12).

text:
Immunization Schedule Principles
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Rather than memorizing a full vaccine-by-vaccine schedule, the underlying principles matter most for exams:

Vaccines are timed to protect infants as maternal antibody protection wanes, and before natural exposure risk rises
Cold chain maintenance (keeping vaccines at the correct temperature from manufacture to administration) is essential to vaccine efficacy
Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) is India’s platform delivering the national schedule free of cost through the general health system — the same primary-care infrastructure discussed in Chapter 11

Geriatric Preventive Screening Priorities
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
Preventive care priorities shift with age — common geriatric screening targets include:

Hypertension, diabetes, and other NCDs (Chapter 7)
Falls risk — a leading cause of injury-related disability in older adults
Cognitive decline — early detection of dementia
Polypharmacy review — older adults are disproportionately affected by irrational medicine use (Chapter 8), given multiple concurrent prescriptions

Fetal Origins of Adult Disease
🟣 MAY KNOW
As introduced in the Nutrition chapter, the Barker hypothesis links poor fetal and early-childhood nutrition to higher adult NCD risk — meaning antenatal and under-five preventive care isn’t only about short-term child survival, but also shapes a person’s health trajectory decades later into adult and geriatric life.

Welcome
Tribal Health in India
Learning Objectives:

Describe the major health determinants specific to India’s Scheduled Tribes
State the burden of sickle cell disease among tribal populations
Explain the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission’s goals
Summarize the Expert Committee on Tribal Health’s key findings
Identify the structural healthcare-access barriers unique to tribal areas

🟢 MUST KNOW · 🟡 SHOULD KNOW · 🟣 MAY KNOW · 🧡 QUESTION

This chapter closes Phase 3 by applying the social-determinants and double-burden-of-disease concepts from earlier chapters to a specific, policy-relevant Indian population group.

title: Tribal Health in India
section: Health Determinants Specific to Tribal Populations
text:
Health Determinants Specific to Tribal Populations
🟢 MUST KNOW
India’s Scheduled Tribes (Adivasi communities) — about 8.6% of India’s population — face a distinct combination of health determinants:

Geographic isolation — habitations scattered across large areas with poor connectivity, transport, and communication
Socio-economic disadvantage — disproportionately represented in the poorest wealth deciles
Undernutrition and anaemia — prevailing at higher rates than the general population (Chapter 9’s malnutrition framework applies directly here)
Genetic disorders — notably sickle cell disease and G-6-PD deficiency, concentrated in specific tribal populations due to historical patterns of inheritance and marriage within communities

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Sickle Cell Disease Burden
🟢 MUST KNOW
Sickle cell disease is disproportionately concentrated in India’s tribal population:

Roughly 73% of Indians carrying the sickle haemoglobin gene (HbS) are from tribal communities — despite tribes being only ~8.6% of the population
Prevalence of the sickle cell trait/disease varies widely by region and community (roughly 1–40% trait prevalence in different populations)
Highest burden concentrated in states including Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, and Assam

Why this matters for prevention: because carrier/disease status can be identified through a simple test, sickle cell disease is a strong candidate for secondary prevention (early detection) at population scale (Chapter 2’s levels of prevention).

title: Tribal Health in India
section: National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (NSCAEM)
text:
National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (NSCAEM)
🟢 MUST KNOW
Announced in the 2023–24 Union Budget and launched by the Prime Minister on 1 July 2023 at Shahdol, Madhya Pradesh:

Goal: eliminate sickle cell disease as a public health problem in India by 2047
Target: universal screening of 7 crore (70 million) people aged 0–40 in affected tribal areas
Provides awareness generation, counselling, and access to affordable, quality care for those diagnosed — through collaboration between central ministries and state governments

This is a direct, named example of a vertical, disease-specific programme (Chapter 11’s terminology) targeted precisely because of the population-specific genetic burden described above.

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Healthcare Infrastructure Gaps
🟢 MUST KNOW
Public health infrastructure in tribal regions is documented to be inadequate, understaffed, and underutilized, with a nationwide shortfall (relative to population-based norms) of thousands of Health Sub-Centres, Primary Health Centres, and Community Health Centres in tribal areas specifically.
Consequence: even where national programmes (NHM, Ayushman Bharat, NSCAEM) exist on paper, their reach into tribal areas is constrained by this underlying infrastructure gap — a reminder that programme design (Chapter 11) and programme reach are separate problems.

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Expert Committee on Tribal Health
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
A four-year study led by Dr. Abhay Bang produced India’s first comprehensive tribal health report, “Tribal Health in India — Bridging the Gap and a Roadmap for the Future,” examining health status, cultural context, and healthcare infrastructure in tribal areas.
Key recommendation theme: addressing the underlying social determinants of tribal health (poverty, education, resource access) is as important as expanding clinical service delivery alone — echoing the social-determinants framing from Chapter 7’s discussion of the social gradient of health.

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Access Barriers Beyond Infrastructure
🟡 SHOULD KNOW
The 2014 Xaxa Commission report identified additional non- infrastructure barriers specific to tribal communities:

Geographical isolation tied to remote/traditional living patterns
Lack of awareness of available health services
Cultural norms and beliefs that may not align with mainstream health-system practices, requiring culturally sensitive outreach rather than a one-size-fits-all delivery model

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Digital-First Screening at Scale
🟣 MAY KNOW
NSCAEM has been noted for a digital-first approach — using digital tools to track screening, testing, and follow-up for a screening programme covering tens of millions of people across geographically dispersed and hard-to-reach tribal areas — an operational adaptation specifically shaped by the geographic-isolation challenge described earlier.

title: Tribal Health in India
text:
Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs)
🟣 MAY KNOW
Within India’s broader Scheduled Tribe population, the government designates certain groups as Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) — communities with pre-agricultural technology, low literacy, declining or stagnant population, and greater isolation than tribal populations generally — requiring even more targeted policy attention than the general tribal-health framework.
